item.title: The Night He Came Home
item.author: Renan Botasse
item.content:encoded: My name is Renan. I lived in Colatina, Brazil.When I was a kid, Halloween did not exist on my street. October arrived hot, with the smell of the Rio Doce in the air and the late afternoon taking its time to go dark. There was no candy at the door, no costumes lined up on the sidewalk. There was, instead, the house we crossed faster, the one someone swore had a story. There were the adults’ warnings: don’t talk to strangers; don’t take long coming back; say where you are. Above all, there was the idea that something could cross the short distance between the gate and the corner and never return a child.In Colatina, “witch” was not a costume imported from an American calendar. It was a word that dropped the volume of a conversation. I still did not know what that meant for real. I only knew that terror did not need a mask to work.Years later, in a dark room, small TV, volume low so the house would not wake up, I reached , John Carpenter’s 1978 film, for the first time. I don’t remember if it was October. I remember the silence after the final credit. I remember thinking that film, shot in a suburb I had never seen, spoke to a fear I already knew: the quiet street, the half-open door, the “why” that never comes. It felt closer to real dread than any story where the monster explains the monster.Maybe no one can fully explain what makes so effective. The most we can do, today, is try to understand a few facts.In cinema, Halloween always existed. In American life, too: candy, costumes, the “haunted house” down the street. In Carpenter’s film, the date is not decoration. It is the thesis.The story begins in 1963, on a Halloween night in Haddonfield. A six-year-old boy kills his own sister. Fifteen years later, in 1978, he escapes a psychiatric institution and returns to town. The film does not invent the slasher, but it organizes the genre with an almost cruel clarity: quiet suburb, teenage girl alone, heavy breathing offscreen, and a man, or what is left of a man, reduced to a silhouette.Carpenter and Debra Hill wrote the screenplay in about ten days. The producers had come to him with the idea of a killer who hunted babysitters. There were rumors the original title would be ; Yablans, one of the producers, denied it. The film was always going to take place on Halloween. Carpenter liked that. It seemed too obvious, and for that very reason, no one had fully embraced the date until then.Haddonfield, Illinois, is fiction. The name came from Debra Hill’s hometown in New Jersey. The county on the police badge points to Bowling Green, where Carpenter grew up. Laurie Strode carries the name of an old girlfriend of the director. Michael Myers, that of a British producer. Tommy Doyle and Dr. Samuel Loomis are Hitchcock echoes: and . Jamie Lee Curtis, in her first film, was the daughter of Janet Leigh. American cinema loves those invisible threads. Carpenter did too.The budget was small, somewhere around $325,000. Donald Pleasence, as Loomis, made $20,000. Jamie Lee Curtis, $8,000. Nick Castle, under the mask, $25 a day. The mask came from a costume shop: a William Shatner face, Captain Kirk, bought for less than two dollars, painted white, the eyes widened. The actors’ own clothes, cars rented from a local dealer, dead leaves reused from scene to scene. Shot in spring, in California, with palm trees hidden in the frame and license plates kept out of the way to fake the Midwest. Robert Englund, years before Freddy Krueger, helped scatter leaves to manufacture autumn.The film made tens of millions. But the number matters less than the feeling it left behind: that evil could live in the empty house at the end of the street, the one every child knows, even without knowing the name of whoever died inside.In real life, after an atrocity, the first question is usually the same: why?The human brain does not tolerate emptiness well. It wants motive, biography, trauma, a bank account, revenge. It wants to turn the absurd into an algorithm. refuses that comfort.Michael Myers, in the credits, appears as . He is not a character in the classic sense. He is a presence. Loomis insists on calling him “it,” not “he.” Evil. A force. Something you watch, fear, try to lock away, and that still crosses the night.There are readings. Michael saw sex too young and could not understand it. Laurie would remind him of Judith, the sister. Tommy, beside her when she drops the key at the Myers house, would be about the age Michael was in 1963. The killings would follow a ritual pattern: bedsheets, an improvised shrine, a body arranged like a scene. All of that may be true. None of it is stated in the 1978 film with the authority of a caption.That is where the film parts ways with so many of its successors. has territory and revenge. A Nightmare on Elm Street has collective guilt. Michael, in the first film, has absence. The mask does not only hide the face: it hides intent. Without expression, we do not know if he enjoys it, if he hates, if he feels nothing at all. Without a “why,” the “what” gets worse.The sequels tried to fill the hole: siblings, curses, supernatural answers. Some of those solutions land. None, to my mind, beats the question left open. Explaining Michael is domesticating him. And domestic fear, the residential street, the half-open door, loses its force when it becomes a manual.Carpenter and Hill also said later that Laurie’s survival was not a prize for virginity, a Freudian reading critics fastened on too quickly. Laurie survives because she pays attention. Because she is not distracted. Because, in the end, she fights back. The rest is couch theory.How you film what has no nameThe film opens with a long shot, almost voyeuristic, through the killer’s eyes. The inspiration points back to Orson Welles’s : a take that forces us to follow the crime as accomplices. At the end, the mask comes off and we see a child. The shock is not only the murder. It is the age.The score, by Carpenter himself, in time signatures his father taught him, does half the work. The story goes that an executive watched the film without the music and did not find it scary. With the score, he changed his mind. A few notes. Enough.Dean Cundey, the cinematographer, and the early use of the Panaglide give the film that restless glide: the camera follows, breathes, does not cut to spare us. The spaces keep getting smaller: street, house, room, closet. At the start, there is a world. By the end, there is creaking wood and almost nowhere left to run.There is also the dry humor of cheap production turning into style. Precarious lighting that swallows detail. The asylum car appearing in the background while Laurie talks. Myers driving with the mask dead straight, an image at once terrifying and absurd. Annie in the laundry room, and us, who saw what she did not, begging in our heads: don’t go that way.The safe suburb, the cliché the film helped crystallize, works because Carpenter films observation first, not the slaughter. Michael is a stalker before he is an executioner. The paranoia builds in the corner of the frame. When the violence arrives, it is already late: the fear came first.Samhain, the haunted house, and what remainsBehind the scenes, people talk about Samhain, the Celtic festival when the dead cross the veil. They talk about evil that cannot be killed. They talk about the Myers house as the haunted house every town invents for itself. Carpenter wanted that universal recognition: the place you walk past faster, without admitting why.Loomis describes Michael with the coldness of someone who spent fifteen years staring into an abyss that stared back. Pleasence took the role after Cushing and Christopher Lee turned it down. Lee would later call that refusal the biggest mistake of his career. In a few days of shooting, a friendship with Carpenter was born that would lead to other films.In the end, Loomis shoots. Six times. In the heart. Michael falls. Then he is gone. The film does not celebrate victory. It offers a montage of empty places, the house, the street, the night, with the breathing still on top. He could be anywhere. Including, the cut suggests, nowhere.It is an honest ending. Because the fear stages is not the fear of a monster with clear rules. It is the fear of explanatory emptiness. The same emptiness that makes a small inland town invent witches when it cannot stand being without a cause. The same one that makes an adult, decades later, remember a street in Colatina at dusk and feel the stomach close, not because of a movie ghost, but because of the old certainty that the dark, there, never needed subtitles.A note, if a note belongsI am not saying a 1978 horror film and the fear of growing up in a small town are the same thing. They are not. One is an artifact. The other is memory. But both, each in its way, deal with the same human difficulty: what to do when the “why” does not come. runs a little over ninety minutes and costs almost nothing on paper. It still scares because it respects the viewer’s intelligence, and because it respects the terror of not knowing. Simplicity. Ambiguity. One night. One street. A white shape walking without hurry.Halloween, on the calendar, is make-believe. In Carpenter’s film, it is a warning.This is the night he came home.And the question that remains, the only one the film refuses to kill along with the victims, is not whether Michael Myers is a man, a demon, or a cheap-production accident.It is another, older, and far less comfortable:If evil needs no reason to cross your street… anyone can be its victim, without warning, without sense, again, without motive.

item.title: US Tech Stocks See Sharp Falls As AI Spending Nears $1 Trillion
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
U.S. technology stocks plunged for a second consecutive day on Friday as investors grew increasingly concerned about the enormous cost of artificial intelligence development and whether those investments will pay off. The Nasdaq fell more than 3.5%, while Intel shares dropped as much as 30%, Reddit fell 26%, and Alphabet extended its losses after shedding more than $500 billion in market value Thursday. The BBC notes that Meta, Alphabet, Oracle, Amazon, and Microsoft have collectively committed to spending $800.6 billion on AI in 2026. From the report: Chris Low, from investment management firm FHN Financial, said the bulk of what was happening in the stock market was in reaction to some of the biggest tech players such as Amazon and Google. He told Reuters the companies were "showing some pretty significant growing pains as they aggressively pursue the AI build-out." "The thinking is that these signs suggest that the entire sector is going to slow down."
Kathleen Brookes, research director at trading firm XTB, said there have been many ups and downs in AI trade in recent months. "Investors have turned ruthless, punishing any signs of disappointment in [third quarter] earnings," she said. "The AI trade has had a good run in recent years, but now investors want payback, and companies like Alphabet and Intel are in the crosshairs." [...] Brookes noted that November is typically a strong month for stocks. "If we see AI stocks continue to struggle in the coming days, it could suggest the AI trade is past its peak, and investors will be looking for a new theme to drive markets," she said.

item.title: GM Reaches $220 Million Settlement Over Selling Drivers' Private Data
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from TechCrunch: General Motors will pay $220 million to 36 states to settle allegations that it illegally sold private driving behavior and location information to data brokers. As part of the settlement, GM must get drivers' express consent before it collects or shares their driving and location data -- terms that are in line with separate agreements it previously reached with California and the Federal Trade Commission (FTC). This settlement does contain a new requirement that GM must have a third party assess the automaker's compliance with the privacy program it has put in place.
The agreement announced Thursday settles a lawsuit brought by a coalition of attorneys general from 36 states that alleged GM had sold the information to data brokers, which in turn then sold it to insurance providers. "This agreement addresses Smart Driver, a product we ended in 2024, and reinforces steps we've taken to strengthen our privacy practices," GM said in an emailed statement. "Safer, more helpful and personalized experiences are enabled by connected vehicle data, and GM is committed to being clear about what information is used, how it's protected, and the choices customers have about what they share."
The settlement comes more than two years after a New York Times report showed how GM and OnStar collected, used, and sold drivers' precise geolocation data and driving behavior to third parties, including data brokers LexisNexis and Verisk. The data was collected through GM's Smart Driver program, a free feature contained within its connected car apps that tracked and rated driving behaviors and seat belt use. Data brokers sold this information to insurance providers, which could affect customers' rates, the NYT reported at the time.

item.title: UK Social Media Ban May Lock Out More Than 100,000 Teens Without ID
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
Under the UK's planned social media ban, more than 100,000 British teenagers aged 16 and 17 could initially be locked out of social media because they lack a passport or driving license that may be needed as a fallback for age verification. The Guardian reports: Ofcom, the UK's online watchdog, said about 150,000 16- to 17-year-olds do not own a passport or driving licence, which are likely to be needed to access age-restricted platforms. The Australia-style ban on under-16s accessing social media services, including Instagram, TikTok and YouTube, is due to come into force next spring. The head of Ofcom, Melanie Dawes, said "motivated children" would seek to bypass the restrictions, as has happened in Australia.
On Thursday, Ofcom published an assessment of age verification measures that could underpin the ban, outlining four "highly effective" methods: checking a person's official ID against a live selfie, a bank verifying an account holder's age, an official digital ID service like the Young Scot card, or estimating someone's age via a selfie. However, the watchdog said a form of official ID would probably be needed as a "backstop" for other methods, such as facial age estimation, which could be inaccurate by several years. Ofcom said a cohort of 16- to 17-year-olds could miss out as a result. "This means that people without a form of photo ID will likely need to take steps to obtain one to access age-restricted services," the regulator said. The report notes that more than nine out of 10 Britons over 16 have passports or driving licenses.
"We should expect that motivated children will seek to bypass the restrictions -- just like alcohol laws can't completely eradicate underage drinking -- but there'll be ways for platforms to mitigate this risk," said Dawes. "This will be a huge cultural shift for our society, so it'll take time to adjust, and everyone will have a part to play."

item.title: Reddit Will Force Everyone to Log In
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
Reddit plans to require users to log in to browse the platform, ending its longstanding practice of allowing anonymous visitors to access posts and discussions. According to CEO Steve Huffman, a key reason behind the decision is to curb unauthorized scraping and automated traffic.
"This is a big change for Reddit, where we've allowed logged-out access to basically all of Reddit for the last two decades," Huffman says. "And I don't know about you, but as someone whose life has been defined by the open internet, it's a big change for me. But I've come to the conclusion that this is the right decision for our platform and the right decision for our business." The Verge reports: There's no definitive timeline on when this change will roll out to all users, or how the site will work if you're logged out. (If I send my friend a link to a thread and they aren't logged in, what will they see?) To start, Reddit will test the logged-in requirement in "select markets outside the US" in the "coming months," according to CEO Steve Huffman. "We'll look at the impact on the user experience, on our business, and on the whole Reddit ecosystem, figure out where the right boundaries are, and go from there." Reddit has also rebuilt and is rereleasing the Reddit app's incognito mode.
Huffman claims the login requirement is better for Reddit's user experience and its ads business and is "more protective of Reddit data." The "vast majority" of unauthorized Reddit access happens "through our logged-out experiences," though the company will still strike licensing deals of its data with companies, like the deals it made with OpenAI and Google in 2024. Huffman notes that Reddit does not need to know a logged-in user's identity -- "Honestly, we don't want to know" -- just that the user is logged in at all. And he says that more logged-in users lets the company deliver "more relevant ads."

item.title: Binance Suffers Biggest Crypto Hack In History With $6.3 Billion Affected [UPDATE]
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
UPDATE 10/30/26: Binance has temporarily suspended customer withdrawals after suffering what investigators say is the biggest crypto hack in history. According to Binance CEO Yi He, the company estimates roughly $6.3 billion in funds were impacted, with roughly $3 billion in assets frozen on-chain so far. Rest assured, "your money is safe, and we're covering every loss," said co-CEO Richard Teng in a LinkedIn post.
"This was a complex attack," said Teng. "The attacker also used a self-destruct mechanism that destroyed tooling and tracers, making it more difficult for us to trace." From a report: Teng said the incident was not carried out by one person. While the initial investigation indicated the involvement of a compromised laptop, further digging revealed additional points of breach. [...] Blockchain analysis firms TRM Labs and Elliptic have linked the theft to North Korean hackers, with TRM attributing it "with high confidence" to a group known as TraderTraitor, the same group responsible for last year's Bybit hack.
Elliptic estimated Friday that about 44% of the stolen assets have been frozen, with stablecoins accounting for nearly all of those funds. The firm estimated that attackers still controlled over $3 billion in crypto that token issuers cannot directly freeze.
The hackers appear to have compromised Binance's wallet-signing infrastructure, allowing them to authorize transactions that drained billions of dollars in cryptocurrency across multiple blockchains, according to the firms. Binance, in its preliminary stage, has conducted an investigation into the hack, which suggests the incident may have begun with a compromised engineer's laptop. The exchange added that it has found no evidence that wallet passwords were leaked. Below is the original story from yesterday, Oct. 29th. Binance is investigating a potential hack after more than $2 billion in crypto was drained from one of its wallets into a new external account, with Blockaid estimating nearly $3.3 billion was moved.
"Our teams are aware of reports of a potential security issue and are actively investigating," said Binance on X.
"User funds are safe," said Binance founder CZ. "It does look like a hack on Binance. Appreciate the quick freeze from Tether (~$971m) and Circle (~$823m). I don't manage Binance anymore, but as a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered."
At around the same time, crypto-based prediction market Polymarket reported its own security incident that wiped out around $2.7 million in user funds.

item.title: The Tragedy of Losing Your Wikipedia Page
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
An anonymous reader quotes an excerpt from a Wired article that explores the often-contentious process of nominating pages for deletion when their subjects fail to meet the encyclopedia's notability standards: What do you need to know -- need to know -- about Xavier Trudeau? The eldest son of former Canadian prime minister Justin, the teenage Trudeau has recently begun performing R&B under the mononym Xav. But, with all due respect to Xav, do those facts make him a person of note? Should you expect to be able to read about him on Wikipedia? What about Evanescence guitarist Tim McCord, or 2012 Yachtmaster of the Year Rainer Holtorff? All three have had a biography on Wikipedia; all three of those biographies were considered for deletion this year on the grounds that the subjects were not notable enough to warrant a biography at all. Every day, dozens, sometimes hundreds, of Wikipedia biographies -- of child actors turned LA realtors, retired ambassadors, soccer players who have played less than 10 minutes of professional soccer -- are purged from the world's free encyclopedia.
It's not as though Wikipedia, which hosts over 7 million articles in the English language, doesn't have the space. But Wikipedia has only so many volunteers to monitor its contents. To this day, Wikipedia editors are discovering hoaxes that have gone undetected for decades. The time it takes to verify the release dates of Xav's three singles is better spent -- the logic goes -- by asking whether the American Civil War officer Nathaniel Lyon really drank mustard during battle, as was claimed in his Wikipedia biography for 17 years. Wikipedia removed the mustard claim, not because it was proven wrong, but because there was no reliable evidence for it. "We're not really looking for what's true," Britta Gustafson, who has been editing Wikipedia since 2001, told me. "We're looking for what's verifiable." Wikipedia editors do not themselves decide that a person is not notable, only that there is a lack of reliable evidence to support the claim...

item.title: How a Bank Serving 100 Million Users Tests Agentic AI in Production
item.author: sarahevans
item.content:encoded: : A KDD 2026 paper follows five customer support AI agents through testing and deployment. The team checks automated graders against expert judgments, starts new versions at 1% to 5% exposure, and tracks whether satisfaction gains come with more self-service or more work for human agents.An automated grader can give an AI agent a passing score and still be wrong. In, engineers at a digital bank report that one grader initially performed worse than simply choosing the most common answer. Before relying on it to evaluate customer-facing agents, they had to improve the evaluator itself.The paper describes how a bank serving more than 100 million users tests agentic AI in production across card delivery, debt management, credit limits, card management and product explanation. That customer base provides context for the deployment; it is not the test sample size.For companies buying agentic AI, the case offers a view into how a team decides an agent is ready to handle more work. The evidence comes from customer support, rather than paid media or back-office workflows. Its useful contribution is the detail behind each readiness decision, from the tests a new version must pass to the point where a person takes over.All Five AI Agents Improved Satisfaction but Scored Below Human BenchmarksAll five agents improved transactional Net Promoter Score (tNPS), collected after a support interaction, in online A/B tests. The comparison varied by agent, including earlier versions and a control group. Scores nevertheless remained below the bank’s expert human-agent benchmarks, which were measured separately within the support funnel.Compared with human agentsSource: Gupta et al., KDD 2026, Table 3. Human scores were measured separately from the AI scores.The self-service rate tracks how many requests the AI resolved without handing them to a person. Card delivery posted the largest gain, 29 percentage points, alongside a 37-point rise in satisfaction. The product explainer was the one exception, with a slight dip the authors attribute to temporary errors in calls to the language model.The Automated Grader Initially Scored Below a Simple BaselineThe team separates an agent’s instructions and business procedures into modules that can be revised individually. Domain experts change those modules, then language models acting as automated graders evaluate candidate versions before live testing.To establish the reference answers, three operations analysts labeled each evaluation sample and explained their decisions. Majority vote determined the final label. Those explanations then helped GEPA, a prompt-optimization method, refine the graders’ instructions.On customer input verification, the initial grader scored 68.88% accuracy. Always choosing the most common label would have scored 77.78%. Optimization raised accuracy to 88.89%, measuring agreement with the expert labels rather than the customer-facing agent’s overall accuracy.The authors also tested whether different grader models agreed after optimization. Those tests covered models from one vendor, leaving broader model coverage for future work.New Agent Versions Start With 1% to 5% ExposureOffline checks let the team test targeted fixes before exposing customers to them. Live metrics then reveal problems those checks missed, including changes in escalation patterns. New versions begin at 1% to 5% exposure while the team tracks self-service, tNPS, escalations and errors.The bank’s agents transfer conversations to people when a request falls outside their routines, necessary data cannot be retrieved or confidence is low. According to the authors, the agents operate within existing policies and human oversight, without unrestricted or irreversible decisions about credit or debt management.Some handoffs can be removed by giving an agent the tools to finish a defined task. In the card-delivery deployment, adding a card-reissue capability removed the need for a human transfer from the most common resolution path. Other handoffs remain part of the operating design.Average handle time can rise even when automation is working. If AI resolves simpler requests, the human team is left with harder cases that take longer.“AI should take the parts of a customer interaction that slow an agent down, so the agent can spend their judgment where it counts,” said Erin Walker, Global Vice President of CX AI, Business & Delivery at TELUS Digital.The company’s framework for also covers adoption and change management. Any routing change lands on the team receiving the transferred cases, and that team needs the customer’s context and the capacity to take them on.A higher satisfaction score can come from sending more difficult cases to people and leaving simpler requests with the AI. Evaluating agentic AI in production therefore means examining why cases escalated. A missing tool and a decision reserved for human judgment call for different responses. The satisfaction score alone cannot show whether the agent improved or the workload moved.

item.title: First Wired XR Glasses Powered By Android XR
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
XREAL has launched the AURA, its first wired augmented reality glasses powered by Google's Android XR platform. They feature transparent Micro-OLED displays, a 70-degree field of view, Gemini AI integration, and a Snapdragon Reality Elite processor. TechPowerUp reports: The device is built around a simple idea: your apps, screens, entertainment, and AI assistant should be able to come with you wherever you go. On day-one, users have access to millions of familiar mobile apps and games from Google Play, alongside many experiences specifically for XR. Android XR brings familiar hand and voice inputs to AURA, while Gemini makes the experiences more natural and intuitive by working across what users see and do.
With Wired Mirroring, users can plug a computer or handheld gaming console directly into XREAL AURA via USB-C and instantly turn it into a massive private spatial window. That means a laptop, handheld gaming device, or other compatible USB-C device can sit alongside native Android XR apps in a user's spatial workspace. Whether turning a plane seat into a private multi-monitor setup, watching a movie on a large virtual screen, or playing Android and console games in an immersive spatial environment, XREAL AURA is designed to make spatial computing practical, portable, and useful.
[...] For work, AURA creates a portable multi-window workspace without requiring a physical monitor. Users can open Android XR apps, mirror a laptop, place windows in virtual space, and use Gemini to help understand or act on what is on screen. For entertainment, AURA becomes a private theater on demand. Users can access familiar streaming apps, expand content into a large virtual display, and use electrochromic dimming to create a more immersive viewing experience while remaining aware of their surroundings when needed. For play, AURA supports Android games and compatible mirrored gaming devices, enabling users to play on a large and immersive private display. The glasses are available to order today, with limited-time pricing starting at $1,099 for the 12GB RAM and 256GB storage model. Devices are expected to begin shipping in mid-November.

item.title: Fed Holds Rates at 3.75%–4.00% in a 10–2 Vote: How QQQ, SPY and Bitcoin Reacted
item.author: Testing MEXC
item.content:encoded: Two officials, Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack, dissented in favor of another quarter-point increase.Markets now see a December hike as likely: CME FedWatch priced an 85.0% chance after the close, up from 78.3% a day earlier, Reuters reported.The S&P 500 rose 0.28% and the Nasdaq Composite 0.27%, and on MEXC the bigger moves in QQQ and SPY contracts came after the closing bell, when Microsoft and Alphabet reported.● The FOMC held the federal funds rate at 3.75%–4.00% by a 10–2 vote, with Cook and Hammack preferring a 25-basis-point hike.● Growth was upgraded to a “strong pace,” and the Fed said it will wait for more information before deciding its next move.● Chair Kevin Warsh did not commit to a hike, but futures moved toward one, with odds rising to 85.0%.● Warsh said one 2027 meeting will become a strategy session with no rate decision, leaving seven rate-setting meetings.● Stocks closed slightly higher, the two-year Treasury yield slipped to 4.722% and the dollar index fell 0.2%.● From 1:55 p.m. ET to the 4:00 p.m. close, QQQUSDT rose 0.38%, SPYUSDT 0.08% and BTCUSDT 0.89%; after the bell, QQQUSDT gave back 0.74% as Alphabet fell.What Did the Fed Decide in October 2026?The Fed left the target range for the federal funds rate at 3-3/4 to 4 percent, according to the FOMC statement.The interest rate on reserve balances stays at 3.90%.Cook and Hammack voted against the decision because they preferred to raise rates by a quarter point; Reuters noted it was Cook’s first policy dissent.The September 16 meeting had raised rates by a quarter point on a 12–0 vote.What Changed in the Fed Statement?The October statement is close to September’s, with three edits that matter.● economic activity is now described as expanding at a “strong pace,” up from “solid.”● the sentence saying the September hike would support a timelier return to the 2% goal.● a line saying the accumulation of more information will help the Committee decide the appropriate policy stance.The Committee kept its line that inflation remains elevated and that it “will deliver price stability.”It also kept describing productivity growth as strong and capital investment as robust, the same AI-era investment that Microsoft and Alphabet reported on a few hours later.What Did Warsh Say About a December Rate Hike?Warsh did not commit to a December move. He said the coming weeks would bring a lot of data that leaves the Committee better placed to decide, according to Reuters.That calendar is crowded: the Q3 GDP report on October 29, the midterm elections on November 3, October payrolls on November 6 and October CPI on November 10.September CPI, the last reading before the meeting, showed inflation at 3.7% from a year earlier, with core at 2.6%.Warsh said politics played no role in the decision, and that he did not think the economy was too hot, although most colleagues disagreed with him.He argued inflation can return to 2% without slower growth or job losses, and that higher rates are already tightening credit, Reuters reported.Why Is the Fed Changing Its Meeting Schedule?Warsh said the Fed will keep eight meetings a year, but some will focus on long-term strategy without a rate vote, Reuters reported.● one strategy meeting and seven rate-setting meetings.● two strategy meetings and six rate-setting meetings.He did not say which meetings will change, and the Fed has not yet published a formal release; its 2027 calendar still lists eight regular meetings.For traders, fewer rate-setting meetings mean fewer scheduled rate-decision days, and more weight on each one that remains.How Did Markets React to the Fed Hold?Wall Street ended slightly higher.● up 0.28% to 7,743.97.● up 0.27% to 26,549.85.● up 0.19% to 52,475.10.The two-year Treasury yield slipped 1.46 basis points to 4.722%, while longer-dated yields rose and the yield curve steepened after the press conference.The dollar index fell 0.2% to 102.15, according to Reuters.Oil stayed in focus: Brent settled 1% higher at $115.32 and US crude 3% higher at $102.78 after an attack on a Saudi refinery, keeping energy at the center of the inflation debate.How QQQ, SPY and BTC Perpetuals Reacted on MEXCOur Fed rate decision preview set four checkpoints for the night: the 2:00 p.m. statement, the 2:30 p.m. press conference, the 4:00 p.m. close and the 00:00 UTC funding settlement.QQQUSDT, SPYUSDT and BTCUSDT 5-minute closes, indexed to 1:55 p.m. ET on October 28, 2026. Source: MEXC public futures API. the first reaction was small. Between the statement and the press conference, QQQUSDT dipped as much as 0.24% from 723.73 USDT and was back at 723.64 by 2:30 p.m. SPYUSDT was 0.08% lower and BTCUSDT 0.09% higher.2:30 p.m. press conference: activity picked up as Warsh spoke. The 2:30 p.m. five-minute bar in QQQUSDT traded about 1.31 million USDT, ten times the hour before it. By the 4:00 p.m. close, QQQUSDT was up 0.38% from 1:55 p.m., SPYUSDT 0.08% and BTCUSDT 0.89%, at 81,544.7 USDT. the larger move came from earnings. QQQUSDT jumped to 728.11 in the first five minutes after the bell as Microsoft rose, then fell to 721.05 by 5:00 p.m. as Alphabet dropped about 10%, a 0.74% slide from the close. SPYUSDT fell 0.29% over the same hour and BTCUSDT 0.31%. QQQUSDT and SPYUSDT both settled at 0% at 00:00 UTC on October 29, unchanged from the previous settlement. Positive funding would have been a cost to longs; the derivatives market added no extra pressure either way.On a Fed night, QQQ moved more after the close than in the two hours after the statement, which shows how much of the index now rides on a handful of megacap reports.Following QQQ and SPY Through MEXCFor eligible users considering share ownership, MEXC RealStocks is a separate route; check availability and supported securities directly.Perpetual contracts do not confer shareholder rights and carry funding, leverage and liquidation risks.Did the Fed raise rates in October 2026?No. The FOMC held the federal funds rate at 3.75%–4.00% on October 28, 2026, by a 10–2 vote. Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack preferred a quarter-point hike.Will the Fed raise rates in December 2026?It is not decided. Warsh did not commit to a move, but CME FedWatch priced an 85.0% chance of a 25-basis-point hike at the December 8–9 meeting after the decision.What changed in the October 2026 Fed statement?The Fed upgraded growth to a “strong pace,” removed the sentence explaining its September hike, and said more information will help it decide its next move.How did QQQ and SPY react to the Fed decision?QQQUSDT on MEXC rose 0.38% from 1:55 p.m. ET to the 4:00 p.m. close and SPYUSDT 0.08%. In the cash market, the S&P 500 closed up 0.28% and the Nasdaq Composite up 0.27%.How did Bitcoin react to the Fed decision?BTCUSDT on MEXC rose 0.89% from 1:55 p.m. ET to 4:00 p.m., to 81,544.7 USDT, then gave back 0.31% in the following hour as tech earnings hit stock futures.How many FOMC meetings will there be in 2027?The Fed will still meet eight times, but Warsh said one 2027 meeting will be a strategy session without a rate decision, leaving seven rate-setting meetings.What is the FOMC interest rate decision?It is the Fed’s announcement of its target range for the federal funds rate after each FOMC meeting; our glossary explains the FOMC interest rate decision in more detail.

item.title: Copy Any Solana Wallet: Blockchain.ai Launches Automated Copy Trading
item.author: Blockchain Wire
item.content:encoded: Discover wallets, check PnL and automatically copy buys and sells on Solana with your own trade sizes and execution limits.Blockchain.ai has launched automated Solana copy trading, allowing users to choose a wallet, set their trade sizes and limits, and automatically follow its buys and sells.A trader buys a token, adds to the position, then sells half while you’re away. Keeping up manually means catching each move, sizing your trade and getting the swap filled. Blockchain.ai automates the process from a funded trading vault using the user’s settings, with copying continuing after the browser tab closes.Find Solana wallets and check their track recordThe includes profiles such as and , alongside other Solana traders. Users can search by name or X handle, inspect associated wallets, or paste a Solana address from outside the directory.Available wallet analytics include trade history, token holdings and 7D, 30D and 90D realized PnL, ROI and win rate. Users can research wallets before connecting their own. For traders with several wallets, copying follows only the specific address selected.The adds token charts, volume and liquidity data, so users can investigate the tokens a wallet trades before funding a copy. Reported PnL excludes unrealized gains and losses and network fees; incomplete trade history can affect the figures.Set trade sizing, slippage and buy limitsScaled sizing follows the share of available trading funds spent by the target wallet. Fixed sizing uses a chosen dollar amount for each new copied buy. Sells follow the proportion of the position sold by the target wallet.For example, if the target wallet spends 10% of its available trading balance, a copy with $500 available would target a $50 buy. A $30 max buy size caps that buy at $30, before fees and execution checks.Users can also set slippage tolerance, maximum price impact and maximum buy delay. Trades outside those limits or failing liquidity and execution checks may be skipped.Manage your vault and open positionsEach copy runs from a separate trading wallet, called a vault, with keys secured through Turnkey. Users can fund a copy with USDC, USDT or SOL. Setup also shows the additional SOL needed for network fees and other on-chain costs.New trades only follows future supported trades. Match portfolio first attempts to buy supported tokens already held by the target wallet at current prices, then follows new trades. Unspent funds stay in the vault.The Copied Traders dashboard shows open positions, copied trades and fill prices. Users can top up or pause a copy. Pausing does not close positions, and transactions already submitted may still confirm.Cash out requests swaps back into the asset used to fund the vault and a withdrawal to the user’s wallet. Withdraw tokens lets users withdraw remaining tokens without swapping them first. Liquidity, execution requirements and network fees apply.Start Solana copy trading on Blockchain.aiPick a wallet. Set your limits. Start copying.Paste a Solana wallet address or explore the directory. Check the wallet’s PnL and trades, choose your budget and limits, then fund and authorize your copy.Copy trading involves risk, including loss of allocated funds. Copied trades can fill at different prices from the target wallet. Timing, liquidity, slippage, fees and skipped trades affect results. Past performance does not guarantee future returns.Blockchain.ai is a crypto analytics and trading platform for token research, Solana wallet tracking and automated copy trading. The platform brings token charts, wallet analytics and trading tools into one interface.Through its Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, Blockchain.ai also connects compatible AI assistants and agents to real-time token prices, liquidity, holder data, transactions and pool data. This lets users bring onchain research directly into their AI workflows. Learn more about the Visit to explore the platform. For product updates and community discussions, follow and join the .Disclaimer: The information provided in this press release is not a solicitation for investment, nor is it intended as investment advice, financial advice, or trading advice. item.title: Proton CEO Is In 'Full AI Psychosis'
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
According to 404 Media, Proton CEO Andy Yen is aggressively pushing AI adoption while fostering what workers describe as a culture of fear that discourages raising security concerns or challenging leadership. The investigation is based on interviews with eight current and one former Proton employees, as well as internal Slack chats, meeting recordings, and an AI manifesto written by the company's CTO. Longtime Slashdot reader devnulljapan summarizes the findings: Engineers at Proton, which makes the encrypted email service Proton Mail and a suite of privacy- and security-focused products, including an encrypted drive service, an authenticator app, and a password manager, are being pushed to "stop lovingly handcrafting all our code and use AI more." Workers describe an environment where employees have genuine concerns about security or being asked to develop security products with AI but feel unable to voice them, lest Yen berates them in front of everyone or threatens their employment at the company. "The CEO is in full AI psychosis and has been for a while now," one of the sources told 404 Media. Yen reportedly dismissed an employee's request for additional security testing before releasing new code, calling it "bullshit and loser thinking" and insisting that "only losers think like that." In a separate exchange over Proton's post-quantum encryption rollout, Yen criticized how the company communicated the feature's limitations and told employees that "perception is more important than truth, the truth doesn't matter if you don't win on perception."
"The train is coming, get onboard or get crushed. Don't be the professional fax machine operator in the internet age," Yen wrote to the security Slack channel. "I think by the end of this year most developers stop programming and start writing specs for tests that AI will code and run, to validate AI written code that humans will no longer be able to review. This will be the last year that we hire engineers, and starting next year we hire what we used to call product managers, to build things with AI."

item.title: AI-Assisted Reconciliation of Enterprise Data: Detecting and Explaining Cross-Platform Discrepancies
item.author: ajaysikharam
item.content:encoded: Deterministic checks find the gaps. AI helps people understand them.Last quarter's revenue was $14.6 million. Or $14.2 million. Or $14.1 million. The ledger says one thing. The Lakehouse table feeding your BI says another. The dashboard the board looked at this morning says a third.None of the three numbers is obviously wrong, and that is the problem. When the same metric lives in several systems, each with its own refresh schedule, transformations and quirks, the numbers drift apart. Reconciliation is the work of finding where they disagree and deciding which one, if any, you trust. Done by hand, it is slow, it misses things, and it scales badly as you add systems.I split the job in two. Deterministic checks establish the facts: row counts, sums, join-key coverage. AI handles triage and explanation. It learns which differences are normal, ranks the ones that are not, and drafts a plain-language account of what probably happened. The checks give you the truth. The AI makes it something a person can act on.Start with checks that cannot lieBefore any model gets involved, you need checks that are plain arithmetic. For every metric you reconcile, run the same small battery of comparisons:Sums of the measures that matterJoin-key coverage, so no business key silently vanishesHash comparisons on a sample of rows, to catch silent corruptionRun them on a schedule. The output is a table of differences with no interpretation. Nothing here needs AI, and that is deliberate. When an engineer asks why a dashboard changed overnight, the first answer should come from a check that can be re-run and gives the same result every time.The trouble with deterministic checks is volume, not accuracy. On a real pipeline they fire constantly, and most of what they flag is expected:Time zone cutoffs make one feed's Fridays look short.Late-arriving rows land after the extract ran.Currency rounding shaves fractions off totals.Two teams define revenue differently, gross versus net, and nobody wrote it down.A dashboard cache lags the Lakehouse by an hour.A human reviewer has to learn all of this, and the knowledge lives in people's heads. Two reviewers disagree on what is worth chasing. Context switching eats hours, and the checks keep firing either way.Let the model learn what normal looks likeThis is where AI earns its place. Feed it the history of past reconciliations, meaning every flagged difference and how it was resolved. Two things happen: A statistical baseline of normal variance for each check tells you that a half-percent gap the morning after a load is routine, while the same gap on a different feed is not.Explanations from history. An LLM gets the current difference plus the closest entries from the resolution log and drafts a short explanation with the evidence attached.Differences that match a known pattern get labeled and logged instead of escalated. The rest are ranked by dollar impact, how new the pattern is, and whether it is getting worse.Reviewers notice the next part most. Instead of a row reading TABLE_A.SALES_TOTAL != TABLE_B.SALES_TOTAL, they get a sentence saying what probably happened and why. Nobody has to decode column names before the coffee kicks in.Go back to the three figures at the top: ledger $14.6M, lakehouse $14.2M, dashboard $14.1M. The deterministic check compares order counts and revenue per fulfillment center between the source system and the lakehouse table:SELECT COALESCE(s.center, l.center) AS center, COALESCE(s.orders, 0) AS source_orders, COALESCE(l.orders, 0) AS lakehouse_orders, COALESCE(s.orders, 0) - COALESCE(l.orders, 0) AS order_gap, COALESCE(s.revenue, 0) - COALESCE(l.revenue, 0) AS revenue_gap FROM (SELECT center, COUNT(*) AS orders, SUM(amount) AS revenue FROM source.orders WHERE order_date >= '2026-07-01' AND order_date < '2026-10-01' GROUP BY center) s FULL OUTER JOIN (SELECT center, COUNT(*) AS orders, SUM(amount) AS revenue FROM lakehouse.orders WHERE order_date >= '2026-07-01' AND order_date < '2026-10-01' GROUP BY center) l ON s.center = l.center WHERE COALESCE(s.orders, 0) <> COALESCE(l.orders, 0) OR COALESCE(s.revenue, 0) <> COALESCE(l.revenue, 0); It returns one row and says nothing about why:The AI layer takes that row and the resolution log. The log shows OH-01 had the same gap on two earlier closes, both traced to the 2 a.m. extract. OH-01 is missing about 12,000 orders (~$412K) in the lakehouse. The source extract ran at 2 a.m., before the late-day batch landed. This matches two earlier closes. Likely cause: extract timing, not data loss. Confidence: medium. Attached: row counts, extract timestamps, and the two prior resolutions.A reviewer re-runs the extract, the gap closes, and the log records the cause as . That explains the $0.4M gap between the ledger and the lakehouse. The dashboard's remaining $0.1M is cache lag, a known pattern, so the model labels it and logs it without escalating.This is the order that works:Name the reconciliation points. For every metric that matters, write down the source system, the lakehouse table and the report. If you cannot name all three, start there.Write the deterministic checks first. Row counts, sums, join-key coverage and hash sampling. Run them on every load, not once a month.Keep a structured resolution log. Every flagged difference gets a row: what it was, its cause category, how it resolved and who closed it. This log is the training data for everything that follows. Variance baselines, prioritization and plain-language explanations.Keep people on the exceptions. Route anything the model cannot explain confidently to a reviewer, with the raw numbers attached. The model drafts and a person signs off.Tradeoffs and where it goes wrongExplanations can sound confident and be wrong: A model can invent a plausible cause for a difference it does not understand. Treat every explanation as a draft attached to evidence and keep the raw check data one click away.The model learns your mistakes. If reviewers wrongly closed a real break as normal, the model will suppress it next time. Spot-check a sample of auto-labeled "normal" differences on a regular schedule.The log is only as good as the discipline behind it. If reviewers close differences with notes like "looked fine", the model learns nothing. Use cause categories instead of free text. The AI layer adds compute, latency and something else to maintain. Small pipelines may not need it. If your checks fire five times a week, a person with a spreadsheet will do better. The layer pays off when the volume of noise exceeds what the team can read.Keep an audit trail of dismissed differences. When the CFO asks why a flagged gap was closed, "the model said it was normal" has to come with the evidence attached.From fire drill to background processMonth-end reconciliation is a fire drill because differences are found late and investigated from scratch. With this setup, the checks run on every load, the noise is filtered and real breaks arrive with a draft explanation. Finance spends less time waiting on the close and more time on the breaks that matter.Pick one metric this week. Write the deterministic checks and start the resolution log. The AI layer can wait until the log has a few months of history. Truth first, explanation second.

item.title: Why Invisible Engineering Work Deserves More Recognition
item.author: Samuel Oladipupo
item.content:encoded: By day I build hospital software. Most of what I do will never be seen by anyone outside my team: a fix to a data import that quietly stopped failing, a migration that went so smoothly nobody remembers it happened, a review comment that stopped a bad pattern spreading. By evening I write in public. A post takes me a few hours and can reach more people in a day than my best code will ever touch directly.Only one of those shows up when someone searches my name. So which one is the real work?It is tempting to pick a side, and plenty of people do, loudly. I think both sides are partly right, and the more interesting question sits underneath them. Researchers have been poking at that question for decades, in car factories, hospitals, universities and open source mailing lists, and what they found is more useful than either side's slogan.The case for the buried builderSome of the most important engineering work is invisible by design. When it goes well, nothing happens. No outage, no incident, no story to tell. The engineer who spends three weeks making a payment flow idempotent has prevented a disaster that will never be written about, because it never occurred.In 2001, two MIT researchers, Nelson Repenning and John Sterman, studied why process improvement programmes kept failing in manufacturing and product development. Their paper took its title from something an engineer at a car company told them: "Nobody ever gets credit for fixing problems that never happened." What they found was a loop. Organisations that rely on firefighting end up rewarding and promoting the people who save the day through heroic effort, rather than the people whose quiet improvement work means there is no fire to fight. Over time, they wrote, senior management increasingly consists of these "war heroes". The system does not just ignore prevention. It selects against it.Healthcare has been wrestling with the same pattern. Patient safety has traditionally been managed by counting what goes wrong and stamping it out. The resilience engineering researchers Erik Hollnagel, Robert Wears and Jeffrey Braithwaite call this Safety-I, and they have argued for a shift to Safety-II: moving from making sure "as few things as possible go wrong" to making sure "as many things as possible go right". Their most quoted line deserves a spot above every engineering team's desk: given how complex the work is, "the surprise is not that things occasionally go wrong but that they go right so often." The catch, as one patient safety researcher put it, is that measuring success is harder than measuring failure. Software has the same problem. We have dashboards for incidents. We have nothing for the ten thousand ordinary days when nothing broke because someone was careful.These developers also carry context no talk can capture. They know why the retry logic has that strange delay, which customer depends on the undocumented field, what broke the last time someone touched the scheduler. That knowledge is load-bearing, and it lives in people who rarely have time to explain it to anyone outside the building.Ten years later it nearly happened again. XZ Utils, a compression library found on almost every Linux system, had been maintained by one person, Lasse Collin, since he wrote it in 2009. In 2022 he wrote on the project's mailing list that his ability to care had been "fairly limited mostly due to longterm mental health issues", adding: "It's also good to keep in mind that this is an unpaid hobby project." Accounts that were almost certainly fake pressured him to hand over control. A helpful new contributor, "Jia Tan", gained his trust, became a maintainer and spent the following year planting a backdoor in the software. It was caught in March 2024 by Andres Freund, a Microsoft engineer who, in his spare time, noticed the new version was using more processing than it should. One invisible worker, burnt out. Another, curious. That was the margin.And the measurement systems around builders mostly miss it. Promotions, job offers and reputations lean on what can be seen and counted. A conference talk is countable. A follower number is countable. "The system did not fall over this year" is not, even when it is the most valuable thing that happened.So the builders have a fair grievance. A lot of real effort goes unrecognised simply because it does not produce anything people outside the team can point to.Invisible work is not evenly distributedThere is a second layer to the builder's grievance: who ends up doing the invisible work in the first place.In 2019, Tanya Reilly gave a talk called "Being Glue" that named something many engineers recognised straight away. Glue work is the onboarding, the roadmap updates, the questions on design documents, the noticing of things that got dropped. It is "the less glamorous, and often less-promotable, work that needs to happen to make a team successful." Her warning was blunt. Managed deliberately, glue work builds technical leadership. Left unconscious, "it can be career limiting. It can push people into less technical roles and even out of the industry."So "good work gets noticed eventually" is not just optimistic. It costs some people more than others.The case for the public developerBut the dismissive version of this argument, that speakers are all talk, falls apart quickly.Many of the developers you see on stage are deep builders. The talk exists because they solved something hard and then did a second hard thing: they made it understandable. Anyone who has tried to explain a gnarly production problem to a room of strangers knows clarity is its own skill. You have to strip the problem to its essence without lying about it, anticipate the questions, and survive the person in the third row who knows more than you.Tanya Reilly's talk is the best example. Glue work existed long before she named it. Thousands of engineers were doing it, unseen. One person on a stage giving it a name did more to get that work recognised than years of it being done quietly. I would not call that all talk. I would call it leverage.So the public developers have a fair point too. Teaching is work. Explaining is work. The industry would be poorer without it.Where each side gets it wrongLegible does not mean loud. It can be a two-line note to your manager: "I found why checkout failed under load and fixed it. It would have hit us during the next sale." That sentence turns invisible work into something a decision-maker can remember. Julia Evans made the same case in her post on keeping a "brag document": some kinds of important work are simply more memorable than others, and the fuzzy work, like improving code review culture or making on-call easier, is the most likely to slip under the radar unless you write it down.The public developer's mistake is quieter. Visibility can slowly become the job. The talks get better while the building gets thinner. Applause starts to feel like feedback on the code, when it is really feedback on the performance. Will Larson has a word for the extreme version: "preening", doing low-impact, high-visibility work. He warns that many companies "conflate high-visibility and high-impact so strongly that they can't distinguish between preening and impact." Being public is fine. Being public about work you have stopped doing is the problem.What the world actually measuresThe world does not measure effort. It never has. It measures what it can see, and it uses proxies: talks, followers, GitHub stars, titles, the size of the company on your CV.Visibility also compounds. In 1968 the sociologist Robert Merton described the "Matthew effect" in science: credit for joint or simultaneous discoveries flows disproportionately to people who are already famous. The rich get richer. Tech works the same way. Once you are the person who gives talks, your next talk is easier to land, your posts travel further, and your ideas get taken more seriously than the same idea from someone nobody has heard of.Measuring harder does not fix it. When McKinsey published "Yes, you can measure software developer productivity" in 2023, Kent Beck and Gergely Orosz responded with a simple model: effort, output, outcome, impact. Their warning was that whatever you measure, people will game. Measure effort and you get busywork. Measure output and you get whatever output is easiest. Their advice was to aim for team outcomes and impact, and to use effort and output only to debug problems. It works as a test for your own work too. "I spent three weeks on the payment flow" is effort. "Duplicate charges went to zero during peak sales" is impact. Only one of those survives a promotion meeting.So the proxies are crude. They reward the visible over the valuable. But they are not random either. Over a long career, the developers I have seen do best are rarely at either extreme. They do deep work, and then they make it legible. A design note that explains a decision. An internal write-up after an incident. A short summary for leadership that turns a technical win into a business one. Occasionally, a public post or a talk.Translating the work without replacing itIf the skill is translation, here is what it looks like in practice, roughly from least effort to most.Write the counterfactual. Prevention work leaves nothing behind to show, so give it something. "Without this, X would have happened, and here is how we know." That one sentence is the difference between "did some refactoring" and "removed the cause of last year's two biggest outages."Keep a running record. A brag document, updated every couple of weeks, is not vanity. It is evidence you will not be able to reconstruct from memory at review time.Move each piece of work one rung up the effort, output, outcome, impact ladder before you share it. Your manager can usually take it the rest of the way.Write internally before externally. An incident write-up or design note reaches the people who decide your career and helps your team. Very often it is also a public post waiting to be edited.If you are doing glue work, say so, out loud, to your manager. Ask whether it counts toward where you want to go. If it does not, get it recognised or hand it to a rota.And if you are the speaker, keep a build log. Check that the thing you talk about is still something you do. If your last three talks are about work from three years ago, pay attention to that.I do not think of any of this as self-promotion. It is closer to documentation: making sure the people who need to understand what happened actually can.None of this is unique to software. A nurse who quietly catches medication errors is doing work that rarely appears in any report, which is exactly what the Safety-II researchers were trying to change. An accountant whose reconciliations stop a problem before the audit gets no credit for the crisis that did not happen. Meanwhile, the colleague who presents well at the quarterly meeting gets remembered. Every profession has its builders and its speakers, and every profession struggles to see the first group clearly.The research keeps landing in the same uncomfortable place. Organisations reward the visible fix over the invisible prevention. They hand the invisible work to the people least likely to say no. Then they are surprised when the systems that depended on that work start to crack, whether it is a factory line, a hospital ward or a compression library on every Linux server in the world.So I will leave you with the question I keep asking myself, whichever side of the line I happen to be standing on that day:If the work you are proudest of disappeared tomorrow, who would notice first: the people who depend on it, or the people who decide what happens to your career next? And if those are two different groups, which one have you been working for?

item.title: What the Heck is Hardcharger?
item.author: Shawn Gordon
item.content:encoded: A while back, I wrote , about Philip Moore's project that took , an in-process library, and turned it into a proper server with concurrent sessions, authentication, TLS, and an Arrow Flight SQL endpoint. It solved a real problem. DuckDB is fantastic, but it lives in your process, and when multiple people or applications need to access the same data, you need something in front of it.Well, the GizmoData folks have gone and replaced it. On October 21, 2026, they announced , a brand new open-source server for DuckDB 2.0, written from scratch rather than ported from the GizmoSQL codebase. It's licensed under Apache 2.0, with no editions or license keys, a notable change I will come back to.Why did Hardcharger ditch Arrow Flight SQL in favor of a new protocol called Chargewire? Why did Phil build it?Arrow Flight SQL runs on gRPC, which means HTTP/2 end to end, gRPC-aware proxies and load balancers, generated code in every client, and no plain browser client at all. GizmoData ran into this running their own cloud: every reload of a shared proxy sent long-lived gRPC connections a GOAWAY, and the next calls failed. Anyone who has tried to put gRPC behind standard infrastructure will recognize that pain.Chargwire keeps the good part of Flight SQL, which is Apache Arrow as the columnar wire format, and throws out the transport. It runs SQL over ordinary HTTP/1.1 and TLS. Results, query parameters, and bulk uploads are Arrow IPC streams, while control messages are small JSON documents. The notes say that version 1.0 is final and will only change by addition going forward.We get some interesting fallout from that design. Short queries are one round trip, so a single POST runs a statement and streams rows back in the same response. Long queries can submit, get a handle, poll, and fetch later, and a dropped download resumes from the batch where it stopped, so no request has to outlive a proxy timeout. Big results can be read as several partitions over separate connections at once. Anything that passes HTTP can pass Chargewire, including curl and a browser's fetch.This is actually pretty nifty when you think about it. You can run a whole query with curl and no driver at all. For anyone wiring up AI agents or quick scripts, that is significantly easier than generating gRPC stubs.The protocol has an OpenAPI 3.1 description that the server itself serves at /chargewire/v1/openapi.json, plus a black-box conformance suite of 282 tests. Chargewire is Apache 2.0 and lives in its own , separate from Hardcharger.The second reason they rebuilt rather than iterated is security. Flight SQL leaves sign-in, sessions, and handle ownership up to each server, so every server has to get them right independently, whereas Chargewire has them in the protocol.Tokens are bearer tokens, not cookies, so a browser never sends a credential on its own and there is no CSRF to deal with. Every handle (sessions, statements, results, uploads) is bound to the identity that created it and checked on every use, so guessing someone else's handle won’t work. Single sign-on runs on the server's own port and certificate, with the server acting as the OIDC provider's confidential client. Under mutual TLS, a client can authenticate with its certificate alone, and tokens issued from a certificate sign-in are bound to that certificate per RFC 8705, so a copied token is useless without the private key.Inside the server, access control is checked within DuckDB against each statement's actual plan, after binding and again before optimizing, so nested SQL, views, and macros cannot route around a grant. If it can’t classify the request, it's refused. They also refuse credential and system files on the host (SSH keys, cloud credentials, the server's own TLS key) at DuckDB's filesystem layer, administrator included.I mentioned the license at the top, and I want to follow up on that tease. In GizmoSQL, access control, instrumentation, and SSO were Enterprise features that required a license key, but in Hardcharger they are included.That means role-based access control with users, roles, and grants down to the column level, managed in SQL with CREATE ROLE, GRANT, and REVOKE. Row policies, column masking, tenants, per-catalog access rules, and Open Policy Agent support. A tamper-evident audit log. Session and statement instrumentation, query profiles, and a Prometheus /metrics endpoint. A statement queue, timeouts, KILL SESSION, and graceful shutdown. There is also a web UI compiled into the binary with a SQL editor, results grid, and schema browser that respects access control, turned on with --web-ui.Going from gated to free is not the direction most companies move. Their stated reasoning is that every team running a shared DuckDB needs these things, which is hard to argue with.There are both package and command-line install options for pretty much any platform. The local version didn’t give me what I needed to solve what I wanted, but the cloud version seems perfect.I want to describe what I wanted to test, though, because I saw this as a real opportunity to solve a problem I have. I have about half a dozen specialized data collectors on my laptop that load data into local DuckDB files. I need to share these with others, but I haven’t found a simple, inexpensive way to do it so far.The one I used for this example pulls my analytics from Medium. They have no good way to get these numbers other than looking at them, and I needed to integrate them with other metrics. The screenshot below is just part of the dashboard I run locally so I can review it, but Claude also has DuckDB skills that let me do what I need with reporting and mixing in other analytics.There are too many steps to detail out here, but using the web interface, it was really simple to load my Medium DuckDB file, and get it available on AWS (they also have Azure and Google Cloud regions). Here is a snapshot of the web console.From here, I launched the SQL Editor for a quick test and previewed the data. I’ve censored the Publication in the result set for privacy reasons.If you look at the previous WebGUI image, you’ll notice an option for AI/MCP. There is an MCP option available for Hardchager, and this is where you can get what you need to include it in something like Claude. You can set your tokens to be read-only, admin, or whatever. For reporting, I just set it to read-only.In this screenshot, you can see that I was able to run a natural-language query on the DuckDB database and get a chart. This is exactly what I needed. I just need to have a daily collection writer and then 'n’ readers.I can’t stress enough how cool this was to get working, and it was extremely simple. I just need to update my data collection Python to write to the remote server now. Drivers cover ADBC for Go, Python, C/C++, R, and Rust; JDBC as a single jar for Java 17 and up with no gRPC, Netty, or protobuf; and a JavaScript client for Node, browsers, Deno, Bun, and Cloudflare Workers.The are very good and provide examples for everything.Hardcharger is nearly perfect for what I need right now, and they are working on the two features I’d like, so I expect to see them soon. The first is to have the cluster auto-spin up on a request. I don’t actually need this running perpetually; the access is very ad hoc. The other is a way to put my data collection apps on their server.So, what the heck is Hardcharger? It is an open-source server that puts DuckDB 2.0 on the network, built on a new HTTP-based protocol called Chargewire that streams Apache Arrow and works with any proxy, load balancer, or curl command you already have. It is the successor to GizmoSQL, rebuilt from scratch, with everything that used to sit behind an Enterprise license key now included. If you have been wanting remote DuckDB with real access control and have not wanted to fight gRPC through your infrastructure to get it, this is worth your afternoon.Check out my other What the Heck is... articles at the links below:

item.title: Can AI Make a Whole Movie From One Prompt? Here's Where It Breaks
item.author: Frank Houbre
item.content:encoded: The question I get most often about AI film tools isn't about price or models. It's this one: can I type my idea and get the movie?No, not in 2026. Every AI video model still generates one short clip per request, and no request remembers the one before it, so a film made of hundreds of shots has to be planned shot by shot before anything is generated. One-click tools can hide that planning from you. They can't remove it.I make Lost Garden, a dark fantasy animated series, mostly alone. Episode 2 runs 21 minutes. It took me 75 hours and about $1,850 in generations. None of those hours were spent waiting for one magic prompt to finish.Here's where the one-prompt idea breaks, and what to do instead.What does a "one-click AI movie generator" actually promise?The pitch is simple and very attractive. Invideo's movie maker page says the tool "turns your movie script into a full-length movie with AI" and makes movie-making effortless "with just a single prompt." Plenty of other sites promise the same thing in different words.Invideo's AI movie maker page, captured on October 19, 2026 (invideo.io).What you usually get is a sequence of short clips stitched together, with a voiceover, music and subtitles on top. For a trailer, an ad or a social video, that can be fine.For a story, the cracks show fast:The main character's face drifts from one scene to the next. between two shots that are supposed to happen in the same room.The camera does whatever it wants, so the edit has no rhythm. without regenerating a whole block.The tool made every decision for you, and you can't take any of them back one shot at a time.Why can't AI video models generate a full movie in one go?Because a single generation is short. Google's own Gemini API documentation for Veo 3.1 lists clip durations of 4, 6 or 8 seconds. You can extend a Veo video by 7 seconds at a time, up to 20 times, for a maximum of 148 seconds. That's two and a half minutes, as one continuous take.Veo 3.1 parameters in Google's Gemini API documentation, captured on October 19, 2026 (ai.google.dev).Other models go longer per clip. Wan 3.0, which we added to ScreenWeaver on October 18, 2026, generates between 2 and 30 seconds. Still nowhere near a film.Single clips and chained extensions next to the runtime of one 21-minute episode.Now do the math on a short episode. Lost Garden episode 2 is 21 minutes, so 1,260 seconds of screen time. At 8 seconds per clip, that's at least 158 generations just to cover the runtime once, before a single retake. And nobody keeps every take.The minimum number of generations for one episode, before any retake.A movie is hundreds of short decisions that have to agree with each other.So the useful question is who makes those 158 decisions, and whether they agree.Why do AI shots forget each other?Each generation request starts from zero. The model doesn't know what it generated for you five minutes ago. It knows what's in the request: the prompt, and any images or video you attach.That's why consistency in AI video always comes from references you pass in, never from the model's memory. If shot 12 and shot 13 show the same knight in the same corridor, it's because you gave both requests the same character reference, the same location reference and a prompt that describes the same light.A one-click tool has to invent those references for you, and it invents them from a two-line idea. It doesn't know that your knight has a lantern for a head, that the corridor is lit from the left, or that this scene is supposed to feel cold. It guesses. Then it guesses again on the next shot, slightly differently.Continuity is information, and a single prompt doesn't carry enough of it. A screenplay does. A shot list does. A storyboard does.What does a working AI film workflow look like in 2026?The workflow that holds up is the old one, with generation moved to the end. Here's the order I use on Lost Garden: Scenes, characters, places, what happens and why. This is the part I never hand to a model. For each shot: framing, angle, camera movement, duration. Short clips stop being a limit when every shot was meant to be short. One image per shot. An image costs far less than a video clip, so this is where you find the bad ideas cheaply. Character sheets, locations, props, attached to every shot that needs them.Generate the footage last, shot by shot, from the storyboard frame and the references. Cut the takes that don't work, regenerate only those shots.Steps 01 to 04 are decisions. Generation comes last.Steps 1 to 4 are where the film gets made. Step 5 is execution.This is also why I'm skeptical of any tool that skips straight to step 5. You save the first hour and lose the next fifty, regenerating shots that were never planned.Where does ScreenWeaver fit in that workflow?I'm a co-founder of ScreenWeaver, so take this paragraph with that in mind. We built it because I was doing those six steps across too many apps, copying prompts from a script file into a generator and losing track of which take belonged to which scene.ScreenWeaver is an AI production pipeline for screenwriters, filmmakers and studios: you write the script, break it into shots, build the storyboard, then generate the footage, all connected to the screenplay. A project has three tabs, Script, Storyboard and Production. Each shot carries what it needs from one tab to the next:, so you always know which line it serves;its framing, angle, camera movement and duration;its character, set and reference images, the same ones from storyboard to video.It doesn't make a film in one click. You write, you cut, you validate your shots, then you generate.The questions people ask us every weekSince the video features went live, the same four questions come back in comments and emails. Here are straight answers.Is ScreenWeaver still in beta?No. The beta ended on October 8, 2026, the day video generation opened to subscribers. The full pipeline (script, storyboard, production) is live for paying plans.The writing side is. The Screenwriter plan is free forever: script editor, outline builder, moodboards, import and export (.fdx, PDF), unlimited projects. Video production is in the paid plans, Auteur at $39.99 a month and Studio at $149.99 a month (prices checked on the site on October 19, 2026). There's no free trial of the paid plans, so the honest way to start is to write your script for free and upgrade when the story holds up.Which AI video model does it use?Several. Seedance 2.5 is the default, and the app also includes Seedance 2.0, Veo 3.1, Kling v3.0, MiniMax H3, Grok Imagine Video 1.5 and Wan 3.0. I don't think one model wins every shot. Lost Garden mixes them depending on what the shot needs.So can it turn my script into a movie automatically?No, and I'd be wary of anything that says yes. It turns your script into a shot list and a storyboard you can direct, then generates each shot from what you approved. You still direct. The tool makes sure every shot remembers what the script said.Can AI make a full movie from one prompt in 2026?No. AI video models generate short clips, from a few seconds to about 30 seconds per request depending on the model, and each request is independent. A full film needs hundreds of planned shots.What is the longest AI video clip you can generate?About 30 seconds per request with today's longest models, such as Wan 3.0. Veo 3.1 generates 4, 6 or 8 seconds and can be extended up to 148 seconds according to Google's Gemini API documentation.How do I keep the same character across AI video shots?Pass the same character reference images into every generation, and describe the same details in every prompt. The model has no memory between requests.What should a beginner do first?Write the script and break one scene into shots before generating anything. One scene of six to ten shots will teach you more than fifty random prompts.If you're about to make your first AI short, start with one scene you've already written, not with a prompt box. And if you want to see what that workflow produces over a whole episode, both episodes of Lost Garden are free to watch.What's the first scene you'd try?

item.title: NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe: A Complete Guide to the Speech AI Model
item.author: aimodels44
item.content:encoded:
NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe 30B A4B is an open-weight, offline speech-and-audio model that turns recordings and text instructions into text. It supports transcription, translation, speaker-attributed and contextual transcription, timestamps, language identification, and audio question answering across 40 languages.
