item.title: AI Won't Replace Marketers: Marketers Using AI Will
item.author: Hongta
item.content:encoded: AI already writes ad variants and routes leads in most marketing teams. The jobs at risk are the ones made up of those tasks, not the people who decide which tasks matter. AI is more likely to replace certain tasks and roles that rely on repetitive execution than marketers who bring strategic thinking to the table.In this post, SotaMedia explores which areas of marketing AI can and cannot replace and how marketers at every career stage, from interns and freshers to managers, can adapt to an AI-driven industry.Why do marketers fear AI can take their jobs?AI can replace marketers to handle many tasks, from creating content and images to automatically analyzing customer behavior and insights based on real-time data. According to the State of Marketing AI, of marketing teams have applied AI in their daily operations. Therefore, the fear of AI is understandable. Here is what AI can do that can outperform marketers.Customer behavior and demands change rapidly. However, traditional campaigns cannot always meet each individual's actual needs and often focus on triggering latent and general needs, which can limit conversion rates.Human marketers cannot manually create thousands of content variations and messages to match different audiences. Meanwhile, AI can create customized messages, emails, and advertisements based on customer data, including browsing behavior, purchase history, location, and payment preferences.If you think AI can only write copy and generate a few images or videos, think again. These are just some of the functions of generative AI tools like Gemini and ChatGPT.Today, AI marketing agents such as Salesforce Agentforce and HubSpot Breeze can analyze customer and campaign data to identify patterns, forecast churn, and predict conversion likelihood. They can even automatically send emails, publish posts, launch campaigns, and optimize campaign performance.AI can produce content faster than human marketers.In the past, marketers took several days to complete a video; now, generative AI like HeyGen can create a short video with vivid images and sound in minutes.Which types of marketers are most at risk of being replaced by AI?AI is unlikely to replace the entire marketing profession, but it can automate many repetitive, execution-focused tasks. Marketers whose roles rely heavily on routine production, manual reporting, or rule-based processes may face greater pressure to adapt.Marketers who rely on repetitive execution: Tasks such as writing template-based SEO articles, compiling reports manually, scheduling posts, and running basic A/B tests can increasingly be automated with AI tools.Marketers who lack strategic thinking: Marketers who follow instructions without interpreting customer insights, evaluating campaign performance, or connecting marketing activities to business objectives may struggle to remain competitive. AI can process data, but human judgment is still needed to define strategy and make business decisions.Marketers who resist adopting AI: Marketers who refuse to learn AI tools can be left behind by their colleagues who use automation to work more efficiently. AI skills have also become a fundamental skill in most recruitment now. Global AI Jobs Barometer, found jobs that require AI skills carried a 56% wage premium.What marketing roles are most likely to be replaced by AI?According to the , AI and automation are expected to reshape jobs involving routine information processing and repetitive tasks. In marketing, the following roles may experience automation, although the extent of replacement will vary by organization and job scope.Junior content writers and basic copywriters: AI can draft SEO articles, product descriptions, email copy, and advertising headlines.Marketing reporting and operations specialists: AI can automate data consolidation, routine reporting, and campaign performance summaries.Entry-level paid advertising specialists: Automated advertising platforms can handle bidding, audience targeting, and routine campaign adjustments.Customer support and chat-based marketing roles: AI chatbots can answer common questions, qualify leads, and provide basic product recommendations.Execution-focused SEO specialists: AI can assist with keyword clustering, content briefs, metadata generation, and routine SEO audits, reducing the need for manual execution.Which field in marketing can AI not replace?AI can automate marketing tasks, but effective marketing still depends on human judgment, emotional understanding, and strategic decision-making. These capabilities help brands build trust, differentiate themselves, and respond to situations that cannot be solved through data analysis alone.Human connection and emotional intelligence.AI can identify behavioral patterns, but understanding why people feel, think, and act a certain way requires emotional intelligence and cultural awareness. Marketers use empathy to develop messages that resonate with audiences and build lasting relationships.Brand campaigns such as Duolingo's mascot-driven social media content and Nike's demonstrate how humor, cultural relevance, and human motivation can shape brand identity. AI can help produce creative assets, but marketers must decide which ideas genuinely connect with their audiences.Strategic thinking and long-term brand vision.AI excels at optimizing individual tasks, such as testing ad copy, analyzing audiences, and adjusting campaign performance. However, marketing strategy requires a broader understanding of business goals, market positioning, competitive dynamics, and long-term brand value.Human marketers make decisions about resource allocation, brand direction, and crisis communication. They also ensure that individual campaigns support the company's wider business objectives rather than focusing solely on short-term performance.Breakthrough creativity and marketing ethics.Generative AI can combine existing patterns to produce new variations, but producing an effective marketing idea requires more than generating content. Marketers must recognize emerging cultural shifts, challenge familiar assumptions, and decide when an unconventional idea is worth pursuing.Human oversight is also essential for evaluating factual accuracy, data bias, copyright risks, and brand safety. Marketers remain accountable for the content they publish and must ensure that AI-generated materials align with ethical standards and audience expectations.Case study: How Pepsi Vietnam used AI to scale marketing without losing the human touchDuring Tết 2024, Pepsi Vietnam incorporated AI into its marketing campaign to speed up creative production and create more personalized consumer experiences. Rather than relying on automation alone, the campaign connected AI capabilities with the emotional significance of returning home for the Lunar New Year.How Pepsi applied AI in its campaignConsumer insights: AI-assisted social listening helped the team identify conversations and emotional themes around family reunions during Tết.Creative production: The team produced 50 key visuals in one week, saving up to $200,000 in creative costs.Media optimization: AI-powered advertising formats improved media cost efficiency by 20%.Personalized engagement: Pepsi introduced an AI avatar mini-app on Zalo, allowing users to turn their selfies into personalized avatars.The campaign reached more than 68 million people and generated over 176 million views. Pepsi also reported a 250-basis-point increase in Tết product volume share compared with the previous year.What can marketers learn from this case?Pepsi's campaign demonstrates how AI can take over time-consuming tasks, including creative production, audience analysis, and campaign optimization. These capabilities allow marketing teams to produce more content and execute campaigns at scale without spending the same amount of time and resources on manual work.However, the technology alone did not define the campaign's direction. The team still needed to understand its audience, develop a message rooted in a relevant cultural insight, and decide how AI could support the campaign's objectives.For marketers, the takeaway is clear: AI can automate execution, but the ability to turn customer insights into effective marketing strategies remains a valuable human skill. Marketers who combine AI proficiency with strategic thinking and emotional intelligence will be better positioned to adapt as the industry evolves.How marketers can thrive in the AI era.To remain competitive, marketers need to move beyond routine execution and learn to combine AI capabilities with human expertise. The skills needed to stay relevant differ by career stage.For freshers and junior marketersMaster AI tools, but understand the fundamentals.Learn to use AI for content creation, research, data analysis, and campaign execution. However, build a solid understanding of marketing principles so you can evaluate AI outputs rather than blindly rely on them.Develop analytical and critical thinking.Go beyond producing content or following instructions. Learn to interpret campaign results, identify performance gaps, and explain why a marketing tactic works or fails.Build hands-on experience with real campaigns.Use AI to speed up execution, but gain practical experience in audience research, campaign planning, A/B testing, and performance measurement. Understanding how these activities connect is more valuable than mastering isolated tasks.For senior marketers and managersStrengthen strategic thinking.Focus on market positioning, customer insights, business objectives, and resource allocation. AI can support analysis, but marketers must determine which problems to solve and which opportunities are worth pursuing.Learn to manage AI-powered workflows.Take ownership of business outcomes.Connect marketing activities to revenue, customer acquisition costs, retention, and customer lifetime value. The ability to make decisions based on business impact becomes increasingly valuable as routine execution is automated.Develop leadership and cross-functional collaboration.Build the ability to align marketing with sales, product, and customer success teams. As AI takes on more execution tasks, coordinating people, technology, and business priorities becomes a key part of marketing leadership.AI is changing marketing, but it cannot totally replace marketers. Marketers whose work is mostly execution face the most pressure; the ones who own strategy and judgment are harder to automate. Instead of fearing AI, marketers should learn how to cooperate with it to handle tasks more efficiently and productively.

item.title: Trump's CTFC Steps In to Defend Kalshi As Utah Brings Criminal Charges Against Execs
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) has sued Utah to defend its claimed exclusive authority over federally registered prediction markets, as the state files (PDF) 14 criminal charges against Kalshi and its co-founders for allegedly violating anti-gambling laws. The Verge reports: On Wednesday, Utah's Attorney General Derek Brown filed charges against Kalshi co-founders Tarek Mansour and Luana Lopes Lara, including 12 counts of online gambling promotion, a third-degree felony, one count of a pattern of unlawful activity, a second-degree felony, and general gambling promotion, a Class A misdemeanor. The civil lawsuit calls Kalshi a "back-alley gambling den," and Attorney General Brown didn't mince words in a statement to Gizmodo.
"Gambling is illegal in Utah, whether you place the bet, run the game, or promote it. Calling it a 'prediction market' doesn't change what it is, and being federally registered doesn't put a company above the law," said Brown. "A federal court has already ruled that Utah's gambling laws apply to Kalshi," continued Brown. "Kalshi kept taking bets from Utahns anyway. That is illegal, and we're putting a stop to it."
[...] The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) has been jumping into action to protect Kalshi and Polymarket by filing lawsuits against any state that brings charges against the betting sites. President Trump's son, Donald Trump Jr., is a paid advisor to both companies. The CFTC announced Wednesday that it was suing the state of Utah as part of its "commitment to maintaining its exclusive jurisdiction over CFTC-registered prediction markets." The argument is that the feds alone should be regulating these sites.
"Utah seeks to shut down prediction markets across a wide variety of markets," CFTC Chairman Michael S. Selig said in a statement. "Event contracts do not just serve hedging and investment purposes -- they also provide the public with information about the outcome of future events. Congress entrusted the CFTC to be the federal regulator with sole responsibility to oversee these markets," continued Selig. "As I've said before, the CFTC has the expertise and responsibility to defend its exclusive jurisdiction over commodity derivatives, and that's exactly what we'll do."

item.title: RAG vs LLM Fine-Tuning: Choosing the Right Approach for Enterprise AI
item.author: Aarti Jangid
item.content:encoded: Generative AI has changed how businesses build intelligent applications, automate workflows, and access information. However, implementing an effective AI solution involves more than selecting a large language model. Organizations must decide how to provide business-specific knowledge, improve response accuracy, and maintain reliable performance as their data grows.Two commonly discussed approaches are Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and Large Language Model (LLM) fine-tuning. Although both can improve AI applications, they solve different problems.Understanding their differences helps development teams select an architecture that meets their technical requirements without adding unnecessary complexity.What Is Retrieval-Augmented Generation?Retrieval-Augmented Generation combines a language model with an external knowledge retrieval system. Instead of relying exclusively on information learned during training, the application retrieves relevant information from a connected knowledge source before generating a response.A typical RAG workflow includes several steps:Business documents are collected and processed.Documents are divided into smaller chunks.Embeddings represent the semantic meaning of those chunks.A retrieval system identifies relevant information for each user query.The retrieved context is supplied to the language model.The model generates an answer based on the available context.For example, an internal employee assistant could retrieve information from company policies, onboarding documents, and technical manuals before answering an employee's question.The primary advantage is that organizations can update their knowledge sources without retraining the underlying language model. However, the quality of responses depends on retrieval accuracy, document quality, and how effectively the model uses the retrieved context.LLM fine-tuning involves further training an existing language model on carefully selected examples to adapt its behavior to a particular task or domain.Depending on the training data and objective, fine-tuning can help a model learn a specific response format, follow domain-specific instructions, classify information, or produce outputs that follow an organization's preferred style.For instance, a company processing thousands of customer support messages might fine-tune a model to categorize requests consistently and generate responses in a defined format.Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning techniques, including LoRA, can reduce the computational requirements of adapting certain models by training a smaller set of additional parameters rather than updating the entire model.Fine-tuning is not the same as connecting a model to a database. It does not automatically provide reliable access to the latest company information, and it should not be treated as a guaranteed way to eliminate hallucinations.RAG vs LLM Fine-Tuning: Key DifferencesThe main distinction is what each approach changes.RAG changes the information supplied to a model when it generates an answer. Fine-tuning changes how a model responds by adapting its learned behavior.RAG is often a strong starting point when an application needs access to frequently changing documents, product information, internal policies, or knowledge bases.Fine-tuning may be more appropriate when the primary requirement is consistent task execution, specialized output formats, or domain-specific behavior that is difficult to achieve through prompting alone.The approaches also have different maintenance requirements. RAG systems require ongoing attention to document ingestion, indexing, retrieval quality, and access permissions. Fine-tuned models require suitable training examples, evaluation, version management, and potentially additional training as requirements change.Neither approach is automatically cheaper or more accurate. Total cost depends on infrastructure, data preparation, inference volume, model selection, and operational complexity.When Should Businesses Choose RAG?RAG is worth considering when the application must answer questions using information that changes frequently.Common use cases include:Enterprise knowledge assistantsCustomer support applicationsProduct documentation assistantsPolicy and compliance information retrievalResearch applications that require source referencesFor example, an enterprise knowledge assistant may need to answer questions using thousands of documents maintained by different departments. A retrieval-based architecture can locate relevant passages and provide them as context for the response.However, adding a vector database alone does not guarantee good results. Teams must evaluate chunking strategies, embedding models, metadata filters, retrieval precision, reranking, and the relevance of the final context.Security also matters. Retrieval systems must enforce document-level permissions so users cannot access confidential information simply by asking the AI assistant a question.When Is Fine-Tuning the Better Option?Fine-tuning may be useful when a business needs a model to perform a repeatable task in a consistent way.Classifying customer messages into predefined categoriesGenerating structured JSON outputsFollowing specialized writing guidelinesExtracting information from recurring document formatsAdapting model behavior to a specific workflowBefore fine-tuning, teams should establish a baseline using a suitable model, well-designed prompts, and a representative evaluation dataset.Training data should be reviewed for accuracy, consistency, privacy concerns, and unwanted bias. The resulting model should then be evaluated on examples that were not included in training.Fine-tuning should be selected because testing demonstrates a meaningful improvement, not simply because the application needs to become more sophisticated.Can RAG and Fine-Tuning Work Together?Yes. RAG and fine-tuning are complementary approaches rather than mutually exclusive alternatives.Consider a customer support application that must answer questions about current subscription plans while following a company's response guidelines.RAG can retrieve the latest subscription details, product documentation, and approved policies. A fine-tuned model can help produce responses in the desired format and tone.A combined architecture may be beneficial when both knowledge freshness and specialized model behavior are important.However, combining both approaches introduces additional complexity. Teams must measure whether the improvements justify the cost of maintaining a retrieval pipeline and a customized model.A practical implementation should begin with the simplest architecture that satisfies the required performance, security, and accuracy standards.How to Evaluate the Right ArchitectureBefore choosing between RAG and fine-tuning, engineering teams should define measurable success criteria.1. Build a representative test dataset. Include common questions, difficult examples, ambiguous requests, and cases where the system should decline to answer.2. Measure answer quality. Evaluate factual correctness, relevance, completeness, and whether responses are supported by appropriate evidence.3. Test retrieval separately. For RAG applications, measure whether the correct documents and passages are retrieved before evaluating the generated answer.4. Assess operational costs. Compare model inference, embedding generation, indexing, storage, training, monitoring, and maintenance costs.5. Test security boundaries. Verify authentication, access controls, data handling, and resistance to attempts to retrieve unauthorized information.6. Monitor performance after deployment. Track failures, user feedback, changes in document quality, and shifts in real-world query patterns.This evaluation process helps teams identify the actual source of poor performance instead of assuming that a different model or more training will solve every problem.Choosing between RAG and LLM fine-tuning depends on the problem an AI application needs to solve. RAG is particularly useful for grounding responses in external, frequently updated knowledge, while fine-tuning can improve specialized model behavior and task consistency.For enterprise applications, the best decision should come from testing representative workloads, measuring operational trade-offs, and evaluating security requirements.Rather than treating either approach as a universal solution, development teams should begin with a clear objective, establish a reliable baseline, and introduce additional architectural complexity only when the evidence supports it.

item.title: Binance pauses withdrawals as hackers suspected of stealing billions in crypto

item.title: Multi-Billion Binance Hack Hitting Crypto Markets
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
Binance is investigating a potential hack after more than $2 billion in crypto was drained from one of its wallets into a new external account, with Blockaid estimating nearly $3.3 billion was moved.
"Our teams are aware of reports of a potential security issue and are actively investigating," said Binance on X.
"User funds are safe," said Binance founder CZ. "It does look like a hack on Binance. Appreciate the quick freeze from Tether (~$971m) and Circle (~$823m). I don't manage Binance anymore, but as a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered."

item.title: Your Billing Migration is Really a State Machine
item.author: naresh goyal
item.content:encoded: A customer opens their inbox and finds two invoices for the same subscription. Another customer shows up in the retention report as a churn, except they never cancelled. Their payment failed, the subscription lapsed in the billing system, and the lapse got recorded as a lost customer.I led the architecture on a migration that produced both of these bugs. A large file-sharing company was replacing its homegrown quoting and billing system with Salesforce CPQ and Salesforce Billing, integrated with Oracle ERP, across hundreds of thousands of customer accounts. The data moved fine. State was the problem.I’m Naresh Goyal, a Salesforce and GTM systems architect with 20+ years in CPQ, billing, and revenue systems. I hold the Revenue Cloud Advanced certification and led the architecture on the migration in this story.Alongside revenue systems work, I've been focused on bringing AI into go-to-market teams. I led AI deployment across a GTM organization, built an AI orchestration platform for revenue workflows, and set up a Salesforce MCP integration with Claude so agents can work directly with CRM data. That work keeps reinforcing the same lesson as this migration: AI agents are only as reliable as the state they read.I’m sharing these lessons because billing migrations usually fail quietly, and most fixes only surface in postmortems.A subscription does not live in one system. Quoting knows what was sold. Billing knows what was invoiced and paid. Provisioning knows what the customer can access. The ERP knows what revenue was recognized. Each system holds a partial copy of the truth, and each one updates on its own schedule.When those copies disagree, the bug lands on a customer. Billing treats a subscription as active and keeps invoicing it after provisioning has shut off access. Or the reverse. The failures we kept hitting were duplicate invoices for one subscription, churn records for customers whose only problem was a failed payment, and provisioning that fired at the wrong moment, granting access before payment was confirmed or withholding it after.None of these are data movement bugs. The records arrived. They arrived carrying state that the receiving system read differently.Our fix started on a whiteboard. Every subscription got an explicit state machine: named states and the allowed transitions between them. Draft, quoted, ordered, activated, suspended, amended, expired, cancelled. A subscription could move from ordered to activated. It could not jump from quoted to invoiced, and any process that tried got rejected instead of quietly writing a bad state.This sounds basic, and most billing systems never do it. State ends up implied by a status field here, a checkbox there, a date that may or may not be set. When state is implied, every integration invents its own reading of it, and you ship the disagreements to your customers.Here is a simplified version of the transition table. The important column is the last one.Order recognized by financeUpsell or downgrade quotedAmendment order recognizedTerm ends without renewalNotice that "payment failed" moves a subscription to Suspended, not Cancelled. That row addresses the false churn problem from the opening. Churn reporting counts Cancelled and Expired, never Suspended, so a failed card no longer looks like a lost customer.Do this on your own migration: list the states, list the transitions, and name the one system allowed to make each transition. If two systems can both push a subscription into the same state, you have found a future incident.The sharpest disagreement sat between billing and provisioning. The legacy setup triggered provisioning off the sales process: a deal closed, a webhook fired, access followed. A closed deal is a sales opinion. The financial system had not yet recognized the order, and sometimes it never did.We rebuilt the handshake around an event. Provisioning fires only when the order product reaches the Activated state, the point where the financial system officially recognizes the order. The trigger is the state change itself. No timer. No scheduled job guessing. No sales stage.Access granted before payment and access denied after payment look like opposite bugs. They have the same root cause: provisioning listening to the wrong signal. Bind it to the financial state and both failure modes close.Before any configuration began, we profiled the full source data, and it was humbling. Thousands of accounts were ghosts. Some had no opportunities at all. Some held closed deals with no products attached. Account hierarchies pointed at parent accounts that no longer existed.Migrating that as-is would have carried every one of those problems into the new platform, where each would have surfaced as a migration defect and burned the team's credibility in the first week. We stopped, cleaned the accounts and repaired the hierarchies with the revenue operations team, and only then started loading.Your source data is worse than you think. The time to find out is before the new system exists, while cleanup is still a data exercise instead of a production incident. If you want a checklist for that first pass, the three questions to ask before any data migration is a good place to start.We did not flip the whole company in one weekend. During the cutover window, the legacy system stayed read-only while both systems stayed in sync. Downstream consumers then switched one at a time: finance first, then provisioning, then the customer success tools. Before each switch, a validation checkpoint compared both systems on the records that the consumer cared about.A phased cutover turns one giant risk into a series of small, checkable ones. When a checkpoint fails, you know which consumer and which record class broke, and the legacy system is still there to compare against. For the checkpoints themselves, this account of proving a 12-million-record migration correct shows what real source-to-target reconciliation looks likeHistorical records carry commercial terms from deals signed years ago. New pricing rules know nothing about those deals. Run a migrated contract through a new pricing engine, and it can reprice a renewal under rules that did not exist when the customer signed.We put a bypass flag on every migrated quote, opportunity, and order. Pricing and product rules check the flag and skip those records, which keep their original terms through a separate legacy price book. New business runs through the live pricing engine. History stays history. It is one more case of a lesson CPQ teams learned long ago: the pricing engine is only as good as the catalog and data underneath it.Revenue schedules were the last piece, because finance owns them and finance does not accept assurances. We migrated the in-progress schedules into rules-based recognition, then ran the old and new systems side by side. The final cutover happened only after consecutive clean cycles, with finance signing off on each one.If your migration touches revenue recognition, build the parallel run into the plan from the start, with a named sign-off at the end of it. It is slower. It is also the only version of that cutover that survives an audit conversation.If you are planning a billing or subscription migration, spend your design time on state. Write the state machine. Decide which system owns each transition. Bind provisioning to the financial event. Profile and clean the source before you configure anything. Cut over in phases with checkpoints, wall history off from new pricing logic, and let finance call the revenue cutover.Once those decisions are made, the data load is close to a weekend job. The decisions are the migration.

item.title: Patrick Stewart, 'Star Trek' Captain and 'X-Men' Superhero, Dies At 86
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
Slashdot readers Cpt_Kirks, eklektic, sconeu, and Vrallis share the unfortunate news of Patrick Stewart's passing. Longtime spokesperson Kelly Bush Novak said Stewart died Wednesday at the age of 86 at his home in Los Angeles following "a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer's disease and Lewy body dementia."
"He has been held in the warm embrace of family and friends, surrounded by live music, prayer, tears, laughter and the kind of profound emotion that only he could inspire after a lifetime of devotion to us all," Bush Novak wrote. "We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace."
The acclaimed British actor became a science-fiction icon as Capt. Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek: The Next Generation and Professor Charles Xavier in the X-Men films. Beyond those iconic roles, Stewart earned multiple Emmy and Golden Globe nominations for performances in Moby Dick, The Lion in Winter, Extras, Hamlet, and Blunt Talk. He later returned to his most famous role in Star Trek: Picard.

item.title: The Zombies of Tech: What Actually Powers the World
item.author: William
item.content:encoded: In Week 9 of the IBM Full-Stack JavaScript Developer track, I stepped back from tutorials and asked a different question: what is the internet actually running on?The answer isn’t the framework that trended on X this morning. It’s older, quieter, and far more stubborn.COBOL: the 67-year-old that moves your money. Created in 1959, COBOL is still widely estimated to sit behind about 95% of ATM transactions and 80% of in-person banking transactions, with some 220 billion lines in production and around $3 trillion in commerce a day. One example: back in 2012, Bank of New York Mellon reported maintaining 112,500 COBOL programs, about 343 million lines of code. The catch is a talent gap. Universities largely stopped teaching it decades ago, and banks are now experimenting with AI tools to help maintain and modernize it.PHP and WordPress: the web’s workhorse. PHP is used by about 70% of websites whose server-side language is known. WordPress, built on it, runs roughly 42% of all websites.jQuery: declared dead, still everywhere. It’s on about 67% of all websites. Even jQuery 1.x, a version from the 2000s, is still found on around 13%.Linux: the invisible foundation. About 62% of websites with an identifiable OS run Linux, and the broader Unix family covers around 92%. Every system on the TOP500 supercomputer list runs Linux too.And the new stuff earns its place. React Native isn’t legacy, but it shows why tools survive: Shopify moved its flagship app to it and now shares about 86% of its code across iOS and Android, up from roughly 5%. Efficiency like that is why a tool lasts. the technologies that last aren’t the newest; they’re the ones that are reliable, and rewriting something that works is expensive and risky. As a developer, learning the new tools matters, but so does respecting the old systems that keep running.What’s the oldest piece of tech you’ve seen still running in production?Sources: W3Techs (2026), Reuters (2017), Computerworld (2012), Shopify’s React Native migration. Usage figures cover only sites where the technology is detectable.

item.title: Beyond Price, What Gives Bitcoin Its Value?
item.author: Evan Ceolini
item.content:encoded: Bitcoin began its history back in the distant 2008–2009. During this time, it managed to transform from an obscure digital currency that was once used to buy pizza into a highly liquid asset. Although the basic principles of Bitcoin have remained the same, its price has changed dramatically during this period.Just a year ago, in October 2025, one BTC was worth about $126,080. And a year later, at the end of October 2026, its price fell by almost 36% — to $81,000. Such “ups and downs” are an interesting phenomenon for me as the CEO of a crypto aggregator. Bitcoin became the starting point for the development of the modern crypto industry, and its price movements influence the mood and dynamics of the entire market.In this article, I’ll look beyond the price chart to explore what gives Bitcoin its value, what drives demand for BTC, and why its role in the crypto market goes far beyond its latest price movements.Value and price answer different questionsThe value of Bitcoin is an individual story. For example, two different people may explain what it consists of in different ways. Someone doesn’t want to use traditional banks for payments or transfers and therefore uses Bitcoin. For another person, it’s more important to have a “reliable” crypto asset with a history and limited supply in their crypto portfolio. These cases are small illustrations of how Bitcoin can be used and what it’s valued for.But value and price are different things. The quoted price is just the price that the buyer and seller come to in each individual trade. One seller takes what the buyer offers, and the next trade may be at a different price. There is no hidden agreed value in dollars behind the quote that you're meant to be able to work out.Thus, it is more difficult to evaluate Bitcoin than a traditional financial asset. Unlike stocks, Bitcoin does not entitle you to any future earnings of a company, nor are there any future cash flows that can be used to determine its value. According to Fidelity, is all about supply and demand. However, that doesn't provide a clear 'fair value' figure.What supports Bitcoin's valueSince 2012, Bitcoin has undergone a approximately every four years, reducing the block subsidy by 50% every 210,000 blocks. Following the April 2024 halving, the subsidy fell to 3.125 BTC per block, down from the initial 50 BTC.What does this tell us? Bitcoin has a capped supply of approximately 21 million coins, while the rate of new BTC issuance declines with each halving. However, as Eswar Prasad argues in his article, , scarcity alone is unlikely to be a sufficient source of value. I agree with this view.. The block subsidy is determined by the protocol rules and block height, rather than by the discretionary decisions of a centralized issuer. Anyone considering buying BTC can examine these rules to understand how the issuance of new coins is expected to change over time.This allows you to take halving into account when assessing the market, but it doesn’t allow you to predict price movements. A reduction in the rate of new BTC issuance alone doesn’t guarantee an increase in Bitcoin’s value: much depends on demand and other market factors. Therefore, when making a decision to buy, it’s important to consider not only the issuance rate but also the possible risks.2. Decentralization and сontrolThe Bitcoin blockchain is so that transactions and blocks are independently verified by network participants. Miners use Proof of Work to propose new blocks, while full nodes check whether those blocks comply with Bitcoin’s protocol rules. Proof of Work makes it costly to rewrite transaction history, which helps protect the integrity of the network and makes it reliable for transferring value.This differs from Arbitrum, which has a different governance structure. Its Security Council has specific emergency powers that allow it to intervene in the network, as demonstrated by the in which it moved ~30,766 ETH held by the KelpDAO to a frozen address. Bitcoin has no equivalent council with the authority to carry out such an intervention.For me, the important distinction is that . Each participant can verify the rules for themselves, but no single participant can unilaterally control the entire network.3. Infrastructure and liquidityWhy do we need money if you can’t buy anything with it? The same goes for Bitcoin. Since its inception, an infrastructure has gradually formed around BTC that allows you not only to store it, but also to buy, sell, and use it for transfers and payments. For example:Of course, as a result, Bitcoin has become much more accessible through exchanges, payment systems, and regulated investment products. But I want to emphasize one important thing: The market quote and the price at which a transaction is actually executed on a specific exchange or exchange service are not the same thing. Liquidity depends on the size of the transaction, market depth, the specific platform, and current market conditions.Is the ‘Digital gold’ argument reasonable?Bitcoin is often compared to gold. For instance, Larry Fink, CEO of BlackRock, has Bitcoin as a way of “digitizing gold.” The arguments in favor of this comparison tend to echo the points I mentioned above. sums them up by pointing to Bitcoin’s scarcity, portability, and divisibility. I think gold works well as a metaphor for explaining Bitcoin’s value, rather than its price, to someone outside the crypto industry.But when it comes to price, the comparison becomes more complicated. Gold has a much longer history as a store of value. In an , the World Gold Council highlighted the difference in price volatility: Bitcoin’s annualized volatility was around 60%, compared with approximately 15% for gold. These figures were based on daily returns in US dollars from December 31, 2018, to December 31, 2023.Why the price moves faster than the networkA coin mined years ago can come onto the market today, that’s why the supply of BTC on the market depends not only on the issuance of new coins but also on the decisions of current holders. You can sell the BTC you bought in an earlier cycle, or you can simply hold on to it.That is precisely why we should not attribute the price increase solely to the halving, since the schedule only answers some of the questions. While we can anticipate changes in issuance volume, we cannot predict how many holders will sell their coins during a price rally, nor how much money buyers will invest. But this isn’t the only factor influencing the movement of the BTC price. I would also highlight other historical events:Monetary policy has an impact on the cost of borrowing and the options available to those holding cash. In 2022, the went from 0–0.25% to 4.25–4.50%, and Bitcoin lost 64.2% (). In other words, 2022 seems to disprove the notion that Bitcoin is immune to the influence of the traditional financial system. We can't actually say how much of that loss was attributable to Fed policy.Access can also be had via the regulator's own decision. When the SEC approved the 2024 ETP listings, they explicitly . A product could be sold through that route without the regulator having to certify that Bitcoin was fairly priced. I'd be very wary of treating regulatory access as a guarantee as to what you should pay.A trader using leverage can control a position which is larger than their own capital. If their collateral is insufficient, then the position may be liquidated. looks at exactly what happens when a string of forced trades hit a thin book with wide spreads.These examples show why Bitcoin's predictable supply schedule is only one part of the picture. Its market price also reflects monetary conditions, regulatory developments, and trading activity.What exactly historical episodes showNear $19,400 in December 2017, about $3,700 at the end of 2018 (). futures launched in December 2017 ().New trading instruments can expand market access without preventing speculative excess or subsequent price corrections.Financing conditions and failures of intermediaries matter alongside protocol design.US spot Bitcoin ETP approval (). Bitcoin's annual gain was 121.5% ().New access channels can change demand without changing the asset's basic rules.Amberdata recorded $6.93 billion in crypto liquidations within 40 minutes ().Forced position closures can amplify a market shock.2017 and 2018 showed the limits of access gave the traders another tool. It didn't in any way give the holders protection against a reversal. I wouldn't blame the subsequent fall on the CME simply because it came after the launch.Terra and FTX are in any account or story about 2022 (alongside the rise in interest rates). goes into detail about how the collapse of both of those businesses had a knock-on effect for others.For Bitcoin holders, dependence on a custodian or a borrower of coins was a real problem. A company that was lending out your BTC was exposing those coins to the risk of the borrower failing to repay. The borrower was, of course, under an obligation to repay. That obligation wasn't just a function of the Bitcoin network producing valid blocks on the blockchain. That's why I draw a clear distinction between the security of the network and the reliability of a business that holds your coins.Figure 3. US federal funds target range for 2022 (annual daily series). Lower and upper limits, percent. Sources: Federal Reserve via FRED,and DFEDTARU. This is a chart of policy timing, not a chart of a measured causal effect on Bitcoin.2024 changed the channels through which demand arrivedIn 2024, two things that were often mentioned in conjunction actually did quite different things.The ETP provided people with a new way to get exposure via securities, while they reduced the amount of new issuance. To treat them as one explanation for the year's return doesn't really explain how much of the buying was via the new channel.To work that out, you'd look at fund subscriptions and redemptions. A higher AUM figure isn't necessarily indicative of new money having come in from investors. The AUM could be higher simply because the BTC that the fund already holds has gone up in value.October 2025 exposed the speed of forced repricing also looked at the orders that were sitting in the market during the October 2025 liquidations. With fewer orders and wider spreads, traders who were forced to exit their positions found themselves in much worse execution conditions. Selling into that market would have added to the fall.The total in the table is for crypto positions (not just BTC), and it's not a measure of an equivalent amount of capital permanently withdrawn from BTC. I take it to be a measure of forced position closures over the period that Amberdata was looking at.Quantum risk: a long-term challenge for BitcoinA more fundamental objection to Bitcoin is of course the risk to the cryptography that underpins ownership. If a holder no longer has confidence in that cryptography, then they have a reason to doubt the asset itself, irrespective of the current state of the market.On 15th October 2026, Google Quantum AI reported on its Willow processor. Magic state cultivation is a technique which produces the low-error quantum states required for fault-tolerant computation and could in principle reduce the amount of hardware required for some computations. Google notes that it still needs to demonstrate the technique at scale.Google's that are powerful enough to break elliptic curve signatures, which authorise spending. This is the real threat, separate from the October lab result. Benzinga's report (as repeated by ) clearly distinguished between a potential future vulnerability and an attack that could be carried out today. The hardware experiment did not demonstrate that Bitcoin had been cracked.Before calling Bitcoin a good long-term investment, we need to understand how this risk will be managed. Quantum-resistant signatures would have to be in the network rules and in the wallet software, and people would have to adopt them. I wouldn’t simply assume that all users will join this initiative just because there is a financial incentive to protect the network.My view on what makes Bitcoin valuableIt’s important to understand that it’s the first cryptocurrency, which laid the foundation for the development of the entire subsequent crypto industry. Today, smart contracts and decentralized applications are being developed on the basis of blockchain technologies.But for me, the value of Bitcoin lies in something else as well. It’s important to me that the network isn’t controlled by a single organization or corporation, but operates on the basis of a decentralized protocol, the rules of which participants can verify independently.Furthermore, Bitcoin is gaining increasing recognition from institutional investors and large businesses. It is no longer just some kind of internet coin, but an asset that has become part of the traditional financial system.Bitcoin is also the first asset I look at when I want to get a sense of the crypto market's mood. It was the first crypto to achieve global prominence. A found an average return correlation of 0.52 between Bitcoin and the other crypto assets from Jan 2018 to Mar 2023. That doesn't mean every other asset moves in line with Bitcoin, of course, but it does give me a reason to use Bitcoin as a benchmark for market sentiment.Author’s note: This article is for informational purposes only and does not constitute financial, investment, legal, or tax advice. Digital assets and DeFi protocols involve significant risks, including loss of principal. Rates, liquidity, availability, and product terms may change, and access may be restricted by jurisdiction. Readers should conduct their own research and assess the applicable terms and risks before using any product or protocol.

item.title: It's Time for Generative AI to Prioritize Understanding Over Communication
item.author: Kelvin Leong
item.content:encoded: Past communication tech conquered physical distance and time. But as generative AI becomes part of how we create, receive, and interpret human messages, it must focus not just on speed and ease, but on reducing the emotional and interpretive distance between people.Communication is one of the most basic human survival behaviors. People communicate to warn others about danger, ask for help, share knowledge, coordinate actions, build relationships, solve conflicts, and make decisions. In modern society, almost every form of collective activity depends on communication: scientific research, business cooperation, education, government operations, family life, and even an ordinary conversation between friends.Therefore, communication has never been only about transmitting information.If communication were simply about moving information from Point A to Point B, then a fax machine would already have solved most human problems.Unfortunately, humans are not fax machines.The deeper purpose of communication is to meet human needs. We need to understand the environment around us, and we also need to understand the people around us. We want other people to understand our intentions, needs, and concerns. At the same time, we must work with people whose knowledge, interests, values, and life experiences may be completely different from our own.So communication looks simple, but in reality it is extremely complex.At the most basic level, the structure of communication is so simple: a sender creates a message, a medium carries it, and a receiver receives and interprets it. For decades, this has been one of the central structures in communication theory.The problem is that two sides of this process are human. And once human beings are involved, things are no longer simple. The sender has their own background, knowledge, motivation, emotional state, culture, and understanding of the situation. Meanwhile, the receiver brings an entirely different set of perspectives, which rarely align completely. The sender may believe a message is perfectly clear because, in their mind, ten underlying assumptions need no explanation. However, the receiver cannot automatically know those unstated assumptions. A word that sounds completely neutral to one person may carry strong emotional weight for another. Humor can be interpreted as playful or as disrespect. Similarly, silence might signal agreement, hesitation, uncertainty, or rejection.Communication technology, as a medium, has been most successful in solving is physical separation.Reducing physical distanceFor most of human history, physical distance was the enemy of communication. The speed of a message depended on how fast a person could travel, how fast a horse could run, how fast a ship could sail, or how quickly a document could be delivered.Modern communication technologies gradually removed this barrier. The telegraph allowed information to cross long distances through electricity for the first time. The telephone allowed human voices to cross distance in real time. Later, computer networks such as ARPANET connected people, machines, and information systems on a larger scale. The World Wide Web then made information stored in different computers and institutions easier to connect and share. After that, email, mobile phones, social media, instant messaging, and videoconferencing made communication faster, cheaper, and more widely available.Today, people across several continents can work together, attend meetings, exchange information, and even maintain long-term relationships, while the delay may be only one or two seconds. From this point of view, communication technology has been very successful in reducing physical distance. But one problem has never been fully solved. Distance has been reduced, but misunderstanding has not disappeared.The reason is not difficult to understand: the most difficult barrier in communication has never been only the distance between two places, but also the distance between two minds.With the arrival of generative AI, the difference between physical distance and mental understanding has suddenly become even more important.Today, people already use generative AI to write emails, prepare meeting summaries, rewrite messages, translate text, adjust tone, explain ideas, and suggest how to reply to others. This creates a basic difference between generative AI and most earlier communication technologies. Telephones, email, and videoconferencing mainly transmit messages created by people. Their job is to move something from one side to another.Generative AI is not only a delivery worker, it also begins to help write the letter. It can help create, modify, and even interpret messages. Hancock, Naaman, and Levy define “AI-mediated communication” as a form of communication in which an intelligent agent modifies, improves, or generates messages on behalf of a communicator.In other words, generative AI can enter both the sending and receiving sides of communication. It can help people overcome language barriers, simplify difficult information, summarize discussions, and identify unanswered questions. These functions are clearly valuable, but this also makes communication more complex.Social media greatly expanded access to information, communities, and public expression. However, greater access did not automatically lead to greater understanding.People interpret information through their own experiences, identities, values, knowledge, and beliefs. This individual perspective does not mean selfishness; it simply means that no two people understand the world from exactly the same position.One example is confirmation bias, the tendency to seek or interpret information in ways that support existing beliefs. Social media can make this tendency easier to express through choices about whom to follow, which communities to join, and which sources to ignore. Recommendation systems can further shape what users see and may contribute to information bubbles and echo chambers. Research shows that both algorithms and user choices can affect exposure to different perspectives, while similar patterns of selective exposure have been observed across other platforms.It would be too simple to argue that social media algorithms created confirmation bias or individualism. They did not. Human beings already had different interests, beliefs, and social identities. The main lesson from social media is that technology can amplify human bias.If the problem of social media is that it helps people select information that matches their existing views, then the problem created by generative AI may go one step further: it may make communication itself more self-centered.Prompt engineering is often described as a way to improve the quality of AI output. This is not wrong but better prompts do not automatically remove the user’s own bias. Instead, they may turn unclear biases, assumptions, and positions into clearer, more precise, and more persuasive instructions. In fact, generative AI can produce a very strong argument in support of the user’s original position, but that does not mean the user understands the other side any better. Research by Cheng and colleagues supports this concern. They found that sycophantic AI systems may excessively agree with users in interpersonal situations, making users more confident that they are right while reducing their willingness to take actions that may help repair conflict.The word ‘generative’ should therefore receive more attention when we think about AI-supported communication.If the internet accelerated how fast we deliver thoughts, generative AI accelerates how fast we produce them. Generative AI can greatly improve productivity, but it can also accelerate miscommunication. This problem matters because failures in communication are not minor technical errors.Many problems in human life can be traced, at least partly, to failures of communication. A misunderstanding between friends can become a long-term conflict because neither person clarifies the original meaning. Repeated communication failure can damage family relationships. Poorly expressed criticism can cause emotional harm that lasts far longer than the conversation itself. In organizations, communication failures can lead to incorrect requirements, duplicated work, weak coordination, and poor decisions. A senior manager may receive a clear presentation without realizing that different teams disagree about the meaning of the underlying data. A company may issue a technically accurate public statement that fails to recognize how customers will interpret it, resulting in a public-relations crisis. In scientific and public communication, misunderstanding can be even more serious. Differences between what scientists mean by terms such as risk, evidence, significant, or uncertainty and what members of the public understand from the same words can affect trust and decision-making.These examples return us to the starting point of this argument: communication exists to serve human needs.If people communicate faster but understand each other less, a central purpose of communication has not been achieved.The next challenge: reducing emotional and interpretive distanceCommunication technologies of the past achieved remarkable success in overcoming physical barriers. Distance became less important. Time barriers became smaller. Transmission costs continued to fall.The next important goal for generative AI should be to reduce emotional and interpretive distance. Emotional and interpretive distance means the invisible gap between what one person truly wants to communicate and what another person finally understands.By emotional distance, we do not mean that technology should make everyone agree with each other. We also do not mean that everyone should feel the same way. A world without disagreement is not only unrealistic. It may not even be desirable.Science needs disagreement. Business needs different opinions. Politics is naturally a place of competing views. Personal life cannot exist without arguments. Different viewpoints can improve decisions and create new ideas. Generative AI should certainly not act as a judge that decides who is right and who is wrong. What should be reduced are unnecessary gaps in understanding. In other words, AI should help people recognize that one sentence may have different meanings. It should identify missing background information. It should separate “what the other person actually said” from “what I think the other person was suggesting.” It should preserve real uncertainty. It should also help both sides understand why they disagree, even if the disagreement remains.Success should not be measured by whether everyone finally agrees. It should be measured by whether both sides truly understand where their disagreement actually lies.For generative AI, this suggests a different path of development.First, success should not be measured only by speed, volume, and efficiency. It should also be measured by the quality of understanding. Generative AI can help people communicate faster. But if misunderstanding also increases at the same time, then being “faster” does not mean very much.Second, generative AI should not become an authority that decides the “correct way to think” or the “correct way to speak.” Generative AI can help people understand how their words may be interpreted by others. But it should not remove reasonable differences in expression simply to create surface-level harmony.Third, AI should be an objective companion rather than the final judge. Its role should be to encourage reflection and broaden the user’s view, rather than deciding what the user should believe.Finally, humans should continue to take an active role in important communication. Choosing a word, asking a question, explaining an idea, or taking responsibility for something that has been said may seem troublesome. But these processes are themselves part of understanding.A different definition of “progress”The history of communication technology is, in many ways, a history of reducing distance.The telegraph separated information from the speed of physical travel. The telephone allowed voices to cross distance. Computer networks connected machines and institutions. The Web connected information on a global scale. Mobile and social technologies made communication increasingly immediate and continuous.Each development made the world physically smaller.Generative AI introduces a different opportunity because it does not only transport human communication. It can participate in creating and interpreting it.This makes the next challenge more difficult, but also more important.If generative AI develops without considering the distance between human understandings, it may automate the problems that already exist. It may allow us to produce misunderstandings faster, defend incomplete interpretations more persuasively, confirm our existing views more comfortably, and distribute poorly aligned messages at unprecedented scale.We may become more connected while becoming less understood.

item.title: Nvidia Chief Seen As Target of Chinese Spy Plot
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from The New York Times: American spy agencies had gathered striking intelligence. A top executive at a Singapore-based data center company was under scrutiny for possibly steering advanced Nvidia A.I. chips to China. And now American officials had concluded that she was a Chinese intelligence asset (source paywalled; alternative source), funneling information to Beijing. But what came next was even more alarming. Surveillance of the executive, Alice Huang or Huang Le, a Chinese citizen, revealed that she had developed a close relationship with Jensen Huang, Nvidia's chief executive.
For years, Washington has worked to deny China the technology needed to match or surpass the United States in the intense global competition for superiority in artificial intelligence. The discovery that Beijing was getting reports from someone with direct access to Mr. Huang, one of the most powerful figures in the A.I. revolution as well as an influential ally of President Trump's, set off alarms at the White House. Roughly a year ago, Mr. Trump was briefed about the intelligence findings, which have not been previously reported, and chose not to do anything with the information. Mr. Trump has been wary of disrupting Nvidia's chip sales, which are helping to drive the economy and the stock market, and of further complicating the trading relationship with China.
This account is based on interviews with people briefed on the surveillance, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because the findings are drawn from classified intelligence, as well as other officials and industry executives and analysts. American officials already suspected that Ms. Huang was helping China evade constraints on its ability to gain access to advanced A.I. chips. But the revelation that she was feeding information directly to Beijing raised more troubling possibilities, including that Mr. Huang had insights into Mr. Trump's thinking on an issue of vital importance to both nations, one likely to come up when the president visits China next month. And it left questions about whether she could be gleaning information about Nvidia, which as much as any company accounts for the lead the United States has maintained in developing cutting-edge A.I. models. The surveillance of Ms. Huang continues, they said, and companies that have been affiliated with her continued this year to purchase Nvidia chips.
Nvidia said in a statement: "Jensen's interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO's job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year." Nvidia is "confident that if the U.S. government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know." Customers like Megaspeed, the company that employed Ms. Huang, "receive ordinary business information -- not sensitive Nvidia trade secrets -- and zero information relevant to national security," the company added.
In a statement to The New York Times, Megaspeed said that its "current leadership" takes the matter "extremely seriously and is committed to getting to the facts behind these allegations." It added that "outside counsel has been retained to conduct a thorough internal investigation and has notified the U.S. government that we are fully committed to cooperating."
