item.title: Alphabet Heads For a $500 Billion Drop In Market Value
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
Yesterday, Google reported its Q3 results that showed searches made through its AI Mode generate less revenue than traditional search, even as overall search revenue grew 12% year over year to $63.25 billion. The news sent Alphabet shares plunging, with Bespoke Investment Group reporting that the stock is on track for its steepest post-earnings decline since the company went public in 2004. Yahoo Finance reports: At its low, Alphabet had lost $524 billion in stock market value, the second-biggest one-day loss ever for a US-listed company. Only Nvidia has lost more, about $593 billion on Jan. 27, 2025, the day China's DeepSeek rattled AI investors. Alphabet would need to close at about $274.75, down roughly 15%, to take Nvidia's record, by Yahoo Finance calculations. It has already blown past the $400 billion SpaceX lost on June 22, the previous No. 2.
In dollars, it's Alphabet's worst day by far. Its previous worst was about $275 billion on July 23. It's also on track for the stock's steepest drop after an earnings report since the company went public, according to Bespoke Investment Group. The previous low was a slide of nearly 10% in July 2008.
[...] US-listed stocks have shed $200 billion or more in a single session 18 times this year through Wednesday. That's up from 13 in all of 2025 and none before 2022, according to Yahoo Finance calculations from Bloomberg data. Alphabet alone has lost about $1.4 trillion since its record in May.

item.title: Cloud vs. Compliance: Resolving the Tug of War over Data Residency
item.author: Poorvy Sharma
item.content:encoded: It is a Gold Standard for customers to know that their Data is in safe hands, but at the same time promise of cloud computing was internet without borders, frictionless, global channel where data flowed seamlessly. This article is based on the experience with working for Cloud Platforms that provide services around the globe. The article focuses to explain that when clients sign the Standard Contractual Clauses with the cloud platform providers, it does not automatically guarantee the data will not cross borders even when the data is stored locally in their region. This is because the Cloud Platforms are dynamic in nature as they take automated backups, integrate with other systems to automate processes. To ensure data privacy it is necessary to use hardware security solutions in the server to ensure no data leaks as well as no entry from back door to the servers. There have been many cases reported for cross border data transfers.For Technical Architects of a Cloud platform, Data safeguarding is one of the key challenges of their day-to-day work. With the increase in the number of cases of identity thefts, every region’s government has to implement regulatory framework to safeguard their citizen’s data.It is very important to understand the difference between Data residency and genuine digital sovereignty. While Data residency is more about the geography where data will be stored or where the castle of data will be built, genuine digital sovereignty speaks more about who has the key to that castle!Deconstructing the Stack: Residency vs. SovereigntyBefore we analyze how modern architectures adapt, we must first distinctly understand the two terms that are frequently confused as inter related: It specifies the physical, geographic location where data will be stored or at rest, processed or backed up. Achieving residency is the first challenge of deciding the physical infrastructure as data residency is a geographic constraint. The physical infrastructure challenge is resolved by building or leasing localized data centers. [1, 2, 3]: In simple terms this is a jurisdictional constraint. It dictates that an organization’s data, metadata, custom code and operational workflows remain governed exclusively by laws of the country data resides in. The data is insulated from foreign extraterritorial access laws (for example the US CLOUD ACT) [1,2,3,4]Data residency may ensure safety when data is at rest, but what happens to data in transit? This question is answered by understanding the below layers that constitute towards true digital sovereignty, further the pyramid image explains the significance of each layer [a][b][c] :1. – The physical location of the data center where data will reside. This makes the base of the pyramid2. Access control (Operational Sovereignty): It means administrative and support activities must be done by trust worthy personnel in the country of Data residency3. Encryption control (Technical Sovereignty): This means that the client holds the key to the encrypted data and hence the service provider cannot fiddle with something they cannot see!4. Legal control of Data (Data Sovereignty): If the software company is headquartered in U.S but stores data in South Africa (that means Data residency is local to South Africa but cloud company is headquartered in U.S) then by lay U.S government can ask provider to hand over the data.Below are few of the major challenges with achieving Digital sovereignty:Every innovation is always posed with challenges as detailed and explained in depth in this article [1]1. The regulations change by region2. Innovations in Technology – We are in the era of AI which changes the equation3. Frequently changing Customer expectations – Data privacy is the major concern for all customers4. Threats to Data security – Hackers are also becoming creative so it is necessary to upkeep the data protection measuresThe market has systematically shifted from centralized public cloud nodes towards highly distributed, isolated and multi-tenant architectures designed for local control. To meet this demand leading global hyperscalers have adopted following engineering strategies [1]:Is it possible to achieve Data Sovereignty just by signing contracts alone? Simple answer to this question is ‘No’; it has to be enforced using hardware and implementing encryption. Most of the platforms have now deployed the models “bring your own key” and “hold your own key”. These models ensure that the cloud vendor, even if they are compelled by the government to surrender the data, encryption makes it unreadable. All this is good when data is at rest and not in the middle of processing, so how do we protect data when it is being processed? Confidential Computing is the answer to this dilemma. The heart of Confidential Computing is the hardware enclave (CPU chip) also technically called the Trusted Execution Environment, this helps separate the data from cloud and decrypts the data for processing within the enclave, so the cloud service provider still does not see any real data. So, in simple statement is secured using encryption, is safeguarded by network protocols like HTTPS, TLS etc. and then is protected by hardware enclave.2. Decoupling and de-risking global infrastructure:To safeguard data in tough situations like war or disconnection due to hardware or network failures, a local version of the cloud can be created to decouple it from global network. Let us understand it with an example: There is a bank headquartered in New York and has a branch in Spain and Norway. If the bank’s main office in NY suddenly experiences network failure, then its branch in Spain and Norway must still be able to operate and service its customers. Decoupling is how this is achieved.3. Balancing global and local partnerships:Innovation is happening around the globe, so enterprises are inclined to partner up with software providers internationally, but to safeguard data they are also partnering with local providers to stay compliant to local data protection governance.It is the responsibility of an enterprise to stay compliant with data protection and should not be considered as a company against cloud implementation. With the fast-growing technology and the era of AI, it is imperative that protecting data should be every country’s top priority. Enterprises need to adapt digital infrastructure to stay ahead in the race while protecting the data. The real challenge is to build a cloud strategy in which innovation, data sovereignty, and trust coexist by design. The real world threats call for well defined data governance strategy, a clear understanding of regulatory obligations, and an architecture that incorporates security, privacy and compliance from the outset. In the age of AI, organizations who build responsible innovation on the foundation of data protection will lead the race!

item.title: REPL While It Works: Inspect a Running Python Program Without Pausing It
item.author: David Kra
item.content:encoded:
Usually, without interrupting it, you cannot interactively debug, call functions in, or change the values of variables in a running python program. This article’s technique removes the limitation.There are plenty of python examples showing how an executing script can interrupt its execution to present a console, where you can interact, and then resume execution. Here, the console is your choice of the Python interactive shell prompt, with its Read-Eval-Print Loop (aka REPL), or alternatively, the python PDB debugger.I wanted to do that interacting, but without the and the parts. While the long running execution continues to run, and without interrupting the program’s flow, I wanted to be able to access objects and invoke other functions concurrently. In the Snow White films, there is a song "Whistle While You Work." (Watch the 1937 version or 2025 version). I wanted to "REPL While It Works.": The audience for this technique is writers of programs that they use for themselves. Normally, a program’s data and functions, their names, semantics, and usage, are not known by others.Achieving this objective is not hard. The main features of the solution are:A convenient repository for pseudo-global objects which can be created, set, and used both by the threads and by you while in the REPL or PDB. Avoid having to use thekeyword.The application’s real work happens in a started thread or threads.The main thread, after any initiation and starting the threads, drops into REPL, or PDB, or both, one after the other.Create a function to hold the pseudoglobal objects as attributes. Add, change, and use them from anywhere. Avoid having to use the keyword.def g(): # This function is never called. # It just holds attributes which can be added, set and used from anywhere. pass # example attributes g.d = defaultdict(list) g.finishedthreads=0 g.startedat=time.time() The application functions, are (a) first defined, and then (b) some of them are started as threads. These do the application’s work. See the details in the below.Drop into the interactive REPL ro PDB console, or one after the other.#This goes at the bottom of the script while True: # Drop into the PDB console print(f'\n Type os._exit() to terminate the process abruptly, without flushing file buffers, running finally blocks, or executing atexit cleanups.') print(f'\n Type sys.exit(0) to terminate the main and daemon threads. It first raises a SystemExit exception in each thread. ') print(" Dropping into the PDB debugger console.") print(" Type c or continue to leave PDB and continue script execution.")
breakpoint()
# Drop into the REPL console print(" Dropping into the REPL console") print(" Type <ctrl>D to leave the REPL and continue script execution.")
code.interact(local=dict(globals(), **locals())) . This is the full program, including the features above.#!/usr/bin/python3 # run multithreaded tasks, with a repl while they run
import code import time from collections import defaultdict import threading import os import sys
# 1 Create the repository
def g(): # This function is never called. It just holds attributes which set and used from anywhere. pass # example attributes g.threads=[] g.glock=threading.Lock() #Global lock available to be used by all threads. g.d = defaultdict(list) g.finishedthreads=0 g.startedat=time.time()
# 2A Define functions
def aworker(i=1,art=0,ep=1,op=1000): wpytid = threading.get_ident() wostid= threading.get_native_id() wname = threading.current_thread().name g.d[i]={"i":i, "name":wname, "wpytid":wpytid, "wostid": wostid} print("Thread started: ",g.d[i]) print(f"Parms = {i=}, {art=}, {ep=}, {op=}") time.sleep(5)
# Resource Lock aquire and use # defined elsewhere: g.glock=threading.Lock() g.glock.acquire() try: # This try - finally avoids deadlocks if what is inside throws an exception print("Acquired ", g.glock) whatever=0 finally: g.glock.release()
time.sleep(50) g.finishedthreads+=1 g.d[i]["Terminated"]=True print(f'Thread terminating {wname}')
def analyze(): pass
def periodicresultssofar(): # started as a thread while True: time.sleep(600) analyze() if g.finishedthreads==g.qthreads: return
# 2b Launch threads
qthreads=12 g.qthreads=qthreads for t in range(1,qthreads+1): w = threading.Thread(name=f'Worker-{t}',target=aworker, args=([t]), kwargs={"ep":1,"op": 3}, daemon=True)
g.threads.append(w) w.start() print(f"Thread Name: {w.name}") print(f"Python Thread ID (.ident): {w.ident}") print(f"OS Native Thread ID (.native_id): {w.native_id}")
# periodic results so far
p=threading.Thread(name=f'PeriodicResultsSoFar',target=periodicresultssofar, daemon=True) p.start() g.threads.append(p) print(f"Thread Name: {p.name}") print(f"Python Thread ID (.ident): {p.ident}") print(f"OS Native Thread ID (.native_id): {p.native_id}")
# 3 Repeatedly drop into the PDB and then the REPL console.
while True: # Drop into the PDB console print(" Dropping into the PDB console.") print(f'\n Type os._exit() to terminate the process abruptly, without flushing file buffers, running finally blocks, or executing atexit cleanups.') print(f'\n Type sys.exit(0) to terminate the main thread and daemon threads. It first raises a SystemExit exception. ') print(" Type c or continue to exit the debugger and let the script continue.") print(" Type analyze() to analyze what has been processed so far") breakpoint()
# Drop into the REPL console print(" Dropping into the REPL console") print(" Type <ctrl>D to exit the REPL and let the script continue.") code.interact(local=dict(globals(), **locals())) How did I use this? I created a multithreaded program which accesses my gmail account. The threads divided up the work of collecting the sender and size of each of the account’s 100K emails. With gmail’s IMAP response time of about 3 seconds per request, it took many hours. This technique let me run my analyze function whenever I wanted even while the data was still being collected. This let me satisfy my curiosity to find the top senders, so far, in terms of total bytes in all the emails for that sender.

item.title: Travala Unveils AVA+ Partners, a New Route to Crypto Payments Powered by AVA
item.author: Chainwire
item.content:encoded: Singapore, Singapore, October 29th, 2026/Chainwire/--, the Binance-backed crypto travel booking platform, today announced AVA+ Partners, a new program that will provide crypto projects with a route to having their token accepted as a payment method on Travala by buying and locking AVA, the token at the heart of the Travala ecosystem.The program, which is currently in development, will require partner projects to hold AVA for as long as their token is accepted on Travala while receiving partner rewards throughout the partnership.AVA+ Partners involves three steps for crypto partner projects:Buy AVA. Partner projects acquire AVA on the open market.Buy NFT. Partner projects acquire a Travel Tiger NFT.Activate & Lock. Partner projects activate a Smart Diamond membership and lock AVA in a dedicated AVA+ Partners smart contract for as long as the project’s token is accepted on Travala.Projects can withdraw from AVA+ Partners at any time. Those that leave the program early contribute part of their locked AVA to the , which Travala has committed never to sell or transfer from. All partner projects are subject to Travala’s approval.“AVA+ Partners turns real-world utility on Travala into a long-term commitment to AVA,” said Steve Hipwell, AVA Foundation Lead Contributor. “It’s a use case that grows directly with the expansion of our partner and payment ecosystem.”The initiative is the latest in a string of joint Travala and AVA ecosystem announcements. AVA locked in AVA+ Partners builds towards the long-term goal of achieving 30% of AVA’s circulating supply locked, with AVA locked by partner projects counted alongside AVA locked through the AVA Smart Program and AVA+ Rewards. Full terms, including withdrawal fees, will be set out in each partner agreement.AVA+ Partners is offered to approved business partners only, under individual agreements, and may be modified or discontinued. This announcement is for information only; it is not an offer, solicitation or inducement to acquire, hold or lock AVA, and is not directed at persons in the United Kingdom, the United Arab Emirates or any jurisdiction where distribution would be unlawful. References to Travala are to TravelFront and its group companies.Founded in 2017 and now backed by industry giant Binance, Travala is the leading crypto-native travel booking service, offering 2,200,000+ properties across 230 countries, 600+ airlines, 50,000+ car rental locations, and 400,000+ activities globally. Travala is a champion of cryptocurrency adoption, accepting over 100 leading cryptocurrencies alongside traditional payment methods. For more information, visit: .The AVA Foundation oversees the AVA token ecosystem, including the AVA Smart Program, AVA token, and Travel Tiger NFTs. The AVA token functions as the key to accessing the AVA Smart Program, which provides travel perks and other benefits to Travala customers, such as AVA payment discounts and AVA loyalty rewards. AVA tokenises the concept of loyalty reward programs using blockchain technology, bringing web3 to traditional loyalty models. For more information, visit: .This story was published as a press release by Chainwire under HackerNoon’s Business Blogging

item.title: Poetry vs uv: Choosing a Python Package Manager
item.author: Michael
item.content:encoded:
Poetry and uv are both Python package managers built to solve the same problem, which is making sure every machine installs exactly the same dependencies. Here’s how the two compare on speed, lockfiles, and day-to-day workflow, and why I now point teams to uv.On a Monday morning, Ada clones a Python project, runs the install command, and the tests pass. On Thursday, Sam clones the exact same commit, runs the exact same command, and three tests fail.Nobody changed a line of code between Monday and Thursday. What changed was the outside world, as somewhere in the project’s dependency tree, unknowingly, a library the project uses had shipped a new minor version on Wednesday night. Ada got the old one while Sam got the new one. The project said “any version above 2.0 is fine”, and both of them were technically right.Every Python developer, to be honest, every developer has lived some version of this. It’s the reason “” is a joke that never stops being funny, and it’s the problem Python package managers like Poetry and uv were built to kill.Recently, I approved a pull request on an open-source Python project I help co-maintain. This PR moved the whole project, all 111 locked dependency versions of it, from Poetry to uv, spanning the local development, CI, release publishing, and the Docker image. The thing I praised in my review wasn’t the speed, although the speed is real; it was a single flag, which was used everywhere. By the end of this piece, you’ll know why that flag matters more than any benchmark.But first, the problem both tools are solving.Think of your project’s dependencies as a recipe.A recipe says “two cups of flour, one stick of butter and a pinch of salt”; it doesn’t say which brand of flour, which batch, or which store to get it from. That’s fine for a recipe; it’s meant to be flexible, and in Python that flexible recipe lives in :[project] dependencies = [ "httpx>=0.27", "pydantic>=2.0", ] means “any version from 0.27 upward”. Today that resolves to one version; next month it might resolve to another and itself depends on other packages which depend on others, each with its own flexible range.A receipt is different; it says exactly what you bought, it tells you the brand, the size, the batch number and the timestamp of when you paid. If you hand the receipt to someone else, they can buy exactly the same things.That receipt is a , it records the precise version of every package in the tree, direct and indirect, plus a hash of each file so nobody can quietly swap one out. Ada and Sam’s problem was that their project had a recipe and no receipt; each of them shopped on a different day and came home with a different brand and batch of flour bought from different stores.Poetry and uv both give you a receipt; they just take very different amounts of time to write it, and they disagree on one important question: what should happen when the recipe and the receipt stop matching?Poetry: The One That Fixed It First.Poetry arrived in 2018, at a time when Python packaging was a pile of separate tools glued together with habit. You used to install things, to isolate them, to pin them, and file to package them, and to upload them. Every project did it slightly differently.Poetry put all of that behind one command line and one file; now you declared dependencies in , it resolved them, wrote a receipt, created a virtual environment for you, and could build and publish your package when you were ready.poetry new myapp # scaffold a package poetry add httpx # add a dependency and update the lockfile poetry install # install everything from poetry.lock poetry run pytest # run a command inside the environment poetry build # build a wheel and source distribution poetry publish # upload to PyPI For a lot of teams, including the project I mentioned earlier, Poetry was the first time Python dependency management felt calm. It deserves real credit for that; it made lockfiles normal in Python and treated publishing a library as a first-class job instead of an afterthought.It also has costs you start to feel as a project grows. Poetry is written in Python, and its dependency resolver works carefully through version constraints. On a small project you would barely notice this, but on a project with a deep tree, resolving and installing can take long enough that you go and make a cup of coffee.It’s one tool among several. Poetry manages your project’s dependencies, but it doesn’t install Python itself. You still need something like to get the right interpreter, and something like to install command-line tools globally. The patchwork got smaller, not gone.Its config was its own dialect for years. Until version 2.0, which was released in early 2025, Poetry kept project metadata under its own section instead of the standard table every other tool reads. Version 2.0 adopted the standard, which helps, but many older projects still carry the old format.None of these are dealbreakers; they’re the kind of friction you stop noticing until something removes it.uv: Same Job, Different Engineuv first appeared in February 2024. It's a Python package manager written in Rust, and it started life as a much faster . It didn't stay that small for long.Today, one uv binary covers what used to take five or six tools:uv python install 3.12 # install a Python interpreter (replaces pyenv) uv init myapp # start a project uv add httpx # add a dependency and update uv.lock uv add --dev pytest # add a development-only dependency uv sync # make the environment match the lockfile uv run pytest # run inside the environment uvx ruff check . # run a CLI tool without installing it (replaces pipx) uv build # build a wheel and source distribution uv publish # upload to PyPI If you've read older comparisons that say uv can't publish packages, that was true in its early months. It isn't anymore. and both exist, and uv now ships its own build backend, . The project I reviewed switched to it as part of the migration.The commands look almost the same as Poetry's, but most importantly, the experience doesn't.uv vs Poetry: The Speed Is Not an ExaggerationRather than quote someone else's numbers, I ran my own. Same machine, same Python 3.12, the same nine dependencies (, , , , , , , , ), with every cache wiped before each round. Three rounds each, median shown: Poetry uv Fresh add, empty cache 22.2s 4.0s Reinstall into a new venv 2.8s 0.11s Both tools installed the same set of packages. The cold run is about five times faster, while the warm reinstall, which is what happens every time someone recreates a virtual environment or CI restores a cache, is roughly 25 times faster. It finishes so quickly the first time that you'll probably check whether it actually did anything.Your numbers will differ with your network, disk, and dependency tree, so run the comparison on your own project, but the gap is consistently large, not marginal.Two things do most of the work.The first is the obvious one: the resolver and installer are compiled code, and they download and unpack packages in parallel.The second matters more day to day. uv keeps one global cache of every package it has ever downloaded, and when it builds a virtual environment, it links files out of that cache instead of copying them. A new environment for a package you've used before is mostly a matter of creating links, which is close to free. Ten projects that all use share one copy on disk instead of ten.Speed isn't really the point.Here's the part most comparisons skip. The headline is "uv is fast," but the bigger change is that you stop thinking about the machinery.With uv, you never have to create a virtual environment, name it, activate it, or remember to deactivate it. notices the project, checks that the environment matches the lockfile, fixes it if needed, and runs your command. You can clone a uv project and type as your very first command, and it will install Python if needed, build the environment, and run the tests.It also handles single files. You can put a script's dependencies at the top of the script itself:# /// script # requires-python = ">=3.12" # dependencies = ["httpx"] # /// import httpx print(httpx.get("https://example.com").status_code) Run it with , and uv builds a throwaway environment with in it. No project, no , no "which venv was this for again?" uv add --script fetch.py httpx writes that header block for you. If you share small tools with teammates, this alone is worth the switch.Since so much of uv's speed comes from the cache, it helps to know how to control it.uv cache clean # wipe the whole cache uv cache clean httpx # remove just one package from the cache uv sync --refresh # re-check package indexes online instead of trusting cached metadata uv run --no-cache ... # ignore the cache completely for this one run The difference between the last two is worth getting right. still uses the cache, but it asks the package index again whether anything new has been published, which is what you want when you know a fix was just released. doesn't read from or write to your cache at all. It uses a temporary directory for that one command, which is useful when you suspect a corrupted download and want to prove it. and tell you how much space it's using and where. On a busy laptop, the answer is often "more than you'd guess," and clears out entries nothing uses anymore.: The Flag I PraisedNow back to Ada and Sam, and to that pull request.uv is built to be convenient, and part of that convenience is that it keeps the receipt up to date for you. If you edit by hand and then run or , uv notices the recipe changed, quietly re-resolves, rewrites , and carries on.On your own laptop, that's exactly what you want.In CI, or in a Docker build, or in a release pipeline, it's a trap. Imagine someone changes a version range in and forgets to commit the updated . A convenient tool fixes it silently in the CI machine's working copy, the build goes green, and the receipt in your repository is now wrong. Nobody notices until someone else's machine resolves something different. That's Ada and Sam all over again, except now you have a lockfile, so everyone believes the problem is impossible. turns that silent fix into a loud failure:It installs strictly from the existing , and if the is out of date with , it refuses and exits with an error. I tested this by changing a project's dependencies without relocking:$ uv sync --locked error: The lockfile at `uv.lock` needs to be updated, but `--locked` was provided.
hint: To update the lockfile, run `uv lock`. Exit code 1. The build stops, and the person who forgot to commit the lockfile finds out in minutes instead of weeks.There are three modes worth keeping straight:uv sync update the lockfile if needed, then install (local development) uv sync --locked fail if the lockfile is out of date, then install (CI, Docker, releases) uv sync --frozen install from the lockfile without checking it (when you trust it completely) does the check on its own without installing anything, which makes a cheap first step in a CI job or a pre-commit hook.That's what I liked about the migration. Every place that installs dependencies in an automated setting- the Makefile targets, the CI workflows, and the Docker build- used . Outdated lockfiles fail out loud instead of being patched up quietly. The tool's convenience stays on developers' laptops, where it belongs, and strictness takes over everywhere else.To be fair to Poetry, it also refuses to install when is badly out of sync with , and does the same job as . The difference is the default. uv leans towards fixing things for you, so you have to choose strictness explicitly. That's not a flaw, as long as you know it's a choice you need to make.When Poetry Still Makes SenseI'm going to point you towards uv, but there are honest reasons to wait.If your project is stable, your team knows Poetry well, installs are fast enough, and nothing hurts, there's no prize for migrating this week. A working toolchain is worth a lot.If you lean on Poetry plugins, for things like dynamic versioning from git tags or exporting in a particular format, check that each one has a uv equivalent before you start. Some do, some need a small script, and some don't yet.And if your release process is deeply tied to and Poetry's publishing flow, budget time to rebuild it rather than assuming it will just carry over.None of these are reasons to stay forever. They're reasons to plan the switch instead of doing it on a Friday afternoon.How to Migrate From Poetry to uvFor most projects, migration is a short afternoon, not a project. The same 111 dependencies came across in the PR I reviewed, with every locked version preserved.There's a community tool that does most of the conversion:It rewrites sections into the standard table, moves development dependencies into , and generates using your existing as a constraint, so you get the same versions you already had instead of whatever's newest today. I ran it on a test project, and it finished in about a second.After that, the work is mostly find-and-replace across the places that call Poetry:poetry install -> uv sync --locked poetry run <cmd> -> uv run <cmd> poetry add <pkg> -> uv add <pkg> poetry add -G dev <pkg> -> uv add --dev <pkg> poetry lock -> uv lock poetry build -> uv build poetry publish -> uv publish Then check the places people forget: Swap the Poetry setup step for uv's, point dependency caching at , and use on every install. Copy the uv binary in, run uv sync --locked --no-dev for production images, and make sure the container starts through the environment's Python rather than a wrapper that no longer exists. Anything that shells out to ., if anyone still needs one. uv export --format requirements-txt generates it from the lockfile, so it never drifts. The README's "getting started" section is the first thing a new contributor runs.Finally, run your full test suite on a clean machine, not just your laptop with its warm caches. Build the wheel, install it fresh, and make sure your command-line entry points still work. The PR I reviewed did exactly that, and the Docker image got its own manual check, because the existing compatibility tests only covered older images and wouldn't have caught a broken build.Back to Monday and ThursdayGo back to Ada and Sam one last time.Their problem was never really about which tool they used. It was that their project had a recipe and no reliable receipt, and nothing stopped the two from drifting apart. Poetry solved that years ago, and it deserves the credit. uv solves the same problem, then removes most of the waiting and most of the separate tools around it: Python installs, virtual environments, global CLI tools, and one-off scripts.If I had to sum it up for a team choosing today, it would be this. Start new projects with uv, move existing ones when you next have a quiet week, and wherever a machine installs your dependencies without a human watching, add , so the day your recipe and receipt disagree, you hear about it immediately instead of three tests and three days later.

item.title: Canada to Join EU Network of Supercomputers
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
Canada is joining the European Union's supercomputing network to give Canadian companies, startups, and researchers access to European computing resources for AI development. The partnership aims to strengthen AI cooperation and reduce dependence on US technology. Politico reports: The EU's supercomputing network is run by the EuroHPC Joint Undertaking, an EU public-private vehicle with an 8.2 billion-euro budget. The network consists of 14 supercomputers (some ranked in the global top 10), 19 AI-focused AI factories and 10 quantum computers. The vehicle will also run seven massive AI data center hubs, known as AI gigafactories, set to be built next year with a total investment cost of 30 billion euros.
Experts praised a possible EU-Canadian compute power team-up, but warned it's only the start. "Compute cooperation is one of the most obvious short-term 'middle power' cooperation plays in AI," said Anton Leicht, technology and international affairs fellow at Carnegie Endowment for International Peace. But he added that for now "it doesn't put a dent into the actual dependence" on the U.S. "As long as the U.S. builds gigawatt-scale clusters, no amount of cooperation that doesn't result in massive buildouts will help," he said.
Canada's engagement in the EU's supercomputer network builds further on Canada's previous partial involvement in the EU's flagship research and development program, Horizon Europe. Horizon Europe partially funds EuroHPC. To date, 38 countries have participated in the EU's supercomputing network: 27 EU member countries plus non-EU countries including Norway, Switzerland, the United Kingdom, Israel and Turkey.

item.title: Frgmnt CEO Aurélien Roussel on How Finance Teams Can Earn Yield on Stablecoins Onchain
item.author: Ishan Pandey
item.content:encoded: Stablecoins have grown to $301.4 billion in DefiLlama's snapshot of 20 October 2026, yet the dollars that a business holds in them earn no lending yield until someone compares lending markets, checks collateral and withdrawal liquidity and arranges custody, which are tasks that sit well outside the usual work of a finance team.Frgmnt is a stablecoin protocol on Base that curates non-custodial Morpho Vault strategies for institutions while its Founding Allocator Program gives an initial cohort of 10 institutional allocators access to those strategies with onboarding through Anchorage Digital, dedicated reporting and regular strategy reviews. Today we sit down with Aurélien Roussel, co-founder and CEO of Frgmnt and former chief operating officer of Bricks.co, to discuss how a finance team decides which part of its treasury belongs onchain, how Frgmnt chooses the lending opportunities behind its strategies and what he hopes to learn from the first ten institutions. Hi Aurélien, welcome to our "Behind the Startup" series. You moved from helping scale Bricks.co to founding Frgmnt. Take us through that journey. What drew you toward stablecoins and how did you decide it was time to build something of your own? My experience at Bricks.co taught me how to build and scale a financial product around a simple idea: making investment opportunities more accessible to a much broader audience. It also showed me that technology alone is not enough. You need a product people understand, a reliable operating model, and above all, trust.When I started looking more closely at digital assets, stablecoins stood out to me. They had already become an important part of the financial system, but much of that capital was still sitting idle or earning yield through fragmented, complex DeFi strategies.I saw an opportunity to bring those worlds closer together: the simplicity and utility of stablecoins with the efficiency of onchain finance. Frgmnt came from that conviction. I wanted to build something of our own that could make this infrastructure genuinely useful, first for individual users and increasingly for businesses and institutions. Why did you choose to build Frgmnt around making stablecoin capital productive? Was there a particular experience or conversation that made the opportunity clear to you and how did you decide what to build first? It was less one particular conversation than a recurring observation: people were adopting stablecoins as a way to hold and transfer dollars digitally, but making those dollars productive often required them to understand multiple protocols, compare rates, manage liquidity, and take responsibility for operational complexity.That creates a gap between what the technology can do and what most users are comfortable doing themselves. For a business, the challenge is even greater because capital allocation also involves internal controls, reporting, and risk management.We decided to start with the core problem: how to allocate stablecoin capital across selected onchain lending strategies without forcing users to manage every underlying position themselves. Frgmnt combines stablecoin infrastructure with a strategy allocation layer designed to assess opportunities and manage allocations as conditions change.The principle is simple: users should not need to become DeFi specialists to access onchain financial infrastructure. Our job is to make that infrastructure easier to use, easier to monitor, and more relevant to real financial needs. A finance team might need to make payments tomorrow while holding other funds for several months. Where does Frgmnt fit into that picture and how would the team use it in practice? The starting point is to recognize that not all treasury capital has the same purpose or time horizon. A company needs immediate liquidity for payroll, suppliers, and operating expenses. Other funds may not be needed for weeks or months.We do not believe all of that money should be treated in the same way. Funds required for immediate payments should remain in appropriate liquid arrangements. For a portion of its treasury that the company can allocate to onchain strategies, Frgmnt can provide access to selected lending opportunities through a more structured interface.In practice, the finance team would assess its liquidity requirements, define the amount it is prepared to allocate, and select a strategy consistent with its risk constraints and investment horizon. The team would then use reporting and ongoing monitoring to follow its positions.The objective is not to replace a company's bank or compromise its ability to make payments. It is to give finance teams another way to manage eligible digital-dollar balances while remaining conscious of liquidity, operational, and smart-contract risks. You have just launched the Founding Allocator Program, initially limited to 10 institutions. Why did you choose to start with a small group and what do you hope to learn by working with the first pilot participants? We deliberately chose a small initial group because institutional adoption requires more than a functioning smart contract. It requires confidence in the process around the product: onboarding, strategy selection, reporting, operational procedures, and communication when market conditions change.Working with ten initial allocators allows us to build those processes closely with the people who will actually use them. We want to understand how their teams evaluate onchain opportunities, what information they need before allocating capital, how they define acceptable liquidity constraints, and what their internal approval processes look like.The program gives participants access to curated Morpho Vault strategies, with dedicated reporting and regular strategy reviews. In return, their feedback helps us improve both the product and the institutional experience around it.We see this as a foundation for long-term distribution, rather than simply a short-term acquisition campaign. If we can demonstrate that onchain strategies can be accessed through a disciplined and transparent process, we can build a much stronger basis for broader institutional adoption. The program includes dedicated reporting, regular strategy reviews and direct access to your team. What will that working relationship look like for an allocator and how will you help its finance team get comfortable with using onchain lending? We want the relationship to feel like a working partnership, not simply access to a vault address. Institutions need to understand what they are allocating to, why a strategy has been selected, and what could change its risk profile.That is why we combine access to selected Morpho Vault strategies with dedicated reporting, regular strategy reviews, and direct communication with our team. The aim is to explain the underlying markets, allocation rationale, liquidity conditions, and the risks that come with onchain lending in language that a finance team can evaluate.Onboarding is also important. Where relevant, we work with partners such as Anchorage to support the institutional access process and help align the setup with each participant's requirements.We do not expect trust to come from a presentation or a headline yield figure. It comes from making the strategy understandable, being transparent about its limitations, and maintaining consistent communication. Our role is to help institutions make informed decisions, not to suggest that onchain lending is risk-free.The Founding Allocator Program extends that route to curated Morpho Vault strategies. Frgmnt states that participants pay no program fees, face no lock-up and can withdraw on the same day under normal operating conditions, with allocations and underlying activity open to review through onchain data as well as dedicated reporting. The program gives participants access to Morpho Vault strategies curated by Frgmnt. How do you choose the lending opportunities behind those strategies and how do you balance the returns participants are looking for with the liquidity they need? We do not look at yield in isolation. A high advertised rate is only useful if the underlying opportunity is compatible with the allocator's risk profile and liquidity requirements.Our assessment considers several factors: the quality and concentration of collateral, market utilization, borrower demand, liquidity available for withdrawals, smart-contract and oracle risks, and the characteristics of the underlying lending markets. We also look at how quickly conditions can change and whether a strategy remains appropriate under less favorable market scenarios.From there, allocation is about balancing competing objectives. A strategy designed for capital that may be needed soon should not necessarily look like one designed for a longer investment horizon. We aim to select and adjust allocations based on both the expected return and the risks required to pursue it.Morpho provides the vault infrastructure, while our curation and allocation approach focuses on selecting suitable opportunities and monitoring their evolution. The goal is not to chase the highest rate at every moment. It is to pursue sustainable, risk-adjusted returns while respecting the constraints that matter to each allocator.No strategy can eliminate market, liquidity, or protocol risk, and we believe that distinction should remain explicit in every institutional conversation. How has the move from COO to co-founder and CEO changed the way you spend your time? What part of building Frgmnt has taught you the most about yourself as a founder? As a COO, I was primarily focused on making the business work: execution, operations, coordination, and turning priorities into concrete results. As a co-founder and CEO, I still care deeply about execution, but I spend much more time deciding what we should not do, where we should focus, and how to build the right relationships for the long term.At Frgmnt, that means balancing product development with institutional partnerships, distribution, risk management, fundraising, and team building. In an emerging market, you cannot simply copy a proven playbook. You have to keep learning while making decisions with incomplete information.The biggest lesson for me has been the importance of focus and credibility. It is tempting to pursue every opportunity in a market as dynamic as DeFi, but a strong business comes from solving a specific problem consistently and earning users' trust over time.Building Frgmnt has reinforced my belief that ambition and discipline need to go together. We want to build a substantial business, but we need to earn every step of that growth through a product that works and relationships that last. Last question. If Frgmnt becomes the company you want it to be, how will a finance team’s working day look different? What will it be able to do with its money that it cannot easily do today? I would like finance teams to spend less time navigating fragmented infrastructure and more time making decisions about their capital.Today, accessing onchain opportunities can mean evaluating multiple protocols, understanding different interfaces, monitoring changing rates, and assembling information from several sources. Those are meaningful barriers for a team whose core responsibility is running a business, not managing DeFi positions.Our ambition is to make that experience much more integrated. A finance team should be able to identify which portion of its stablecoin balances is suitable for deployment, understand the strategy and its risks, access the relevant infrastructure, and monitor its positions through clear reporting.Over time, we want Frgmnt to become a bridge between stablecoins and institutional treasury management: combining strategy allocation, onchain infrastructure, and a more familiar operating experience.Ultimately, making money productive should not require businesses to become experts in every layer of the technology. We want to give them more choice over how they manage digital-dollar liquidity, with the transparency to understand what they are doing and the controls to make decisions responsibly.Don’t forget to like and share the story!

item.title: DoorDash Strikes $17 Billion Deal For US Rival Instacart
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
DoorDash has agreed to acquire Instacart for about $17 billion as it expands beyond restaurant delivery and deeper into the U.S. grocery market. The deal, expected to close in late 2027 or the first half of 2028, could face regulatory scrutiny over further consolidation in the delivery industry. Reuters reports: DoorDash has offered Instacart shareholders $65 per share held, representing a premium of about 26% to the stock's closing price on October 22 before reports of deal talks first emerged. The consideration will be at least 75% cash, with Instacart shareholders able to elect cash, DoorDash stock or a combination of the two, the companies said.
[...] The transaction is expected to close at the end of 2027 or the first half of 2028. The deal could face scrutiny over its impact on competition, with New York City's Department of Consumer and Worker Protection (DCWP) saying on Wednesday that a potential merger continued a "troubling trend" of corporate consolidation. DoorDash, however, pledged on Thursday that local grocers could continue to work with any delivery platform they choose.

item.title: Building a Docs-as-Code Workflow With Markdown, Mermaid, and GitHub Actions
item.author: Himashi Meththasena
item.content:encoded: Every engineering team starts with noble intentions. A new project launches, and a sleek Notion page or Confluence space is created. Architecture diagrams are drawn, API contracts are detailed, and onboarding guides are carefully written.The codebase has evolved through dozens of pull requests, hotfixes, and refactors. The documentation, however, remains frozen in time. New developers join the team, follow the setup guide, hit four cryptic setup errors on step two, and realize the docs are a lie.We’ve all experienced this phenomenon: . Traditional static wikis fail because they live completely detached from where engineers actually spend their time: the code.Here is how we killed our rotting internal wiki and built a sustainable, auto-updating "Code-First" documentation ecosystem that engineers actually maintain.The Root Cause: Why Traditional Wikis FailBefore changing our workflow, we analyzed why our team constantly abandoned Notion and Confluence:Context Switching Friction: Updating a wiki requires opening a browser tab, finding the right page (out of hundreds of stale ones), and manually syncing code changes. Under deadline pressure, documentation is always the first task dropped.Zero Quality Control or CI Validation: There is no pull request process for wikis. Code gets tested, reviewed, and block-checked by CI/CD, while documentation lives in an unversioned void where anyone can break accuracy without feedback.Out-of-Sync Architectural Diagrams: Diagrams drawn in external UI tools become obsolete the moment a microservice endpoint changes or a new message queue is added.The Solution: The "Code-First Docs" ArchitectureWe decided to treat documentation as a first-class citizen of our codebase. If code changes, the documentation changes in the exact same Git commit.Here are the three pillars we implemented to make Docs-as-Code work at scale:1. Markdown Co-located with Source CodeInstead of centralized external wikis, every repository owns its documentation. High-level architecture, setup guides, and troubleshooting runbooks live inside a directory right next to the source code.├── .github/ │ └── workflows/ │ └── docs-ci.yml ├── docs/ │ ├── architecture.md │ ├── onboarding.md │ └── runbooks/ │ └── high-cpu-troubleshooting.md ├── src/ └── README.md 2. Automated API and Architecture Diagram GenerationWe stopped manually drawing architecture diagrams and writing API specs by hand. Instead, we generate them programmatically: We use embedded directly inside Markdown files. When a system flow changes, engineers update simple text definitions rather than dragging shapes in a UI tool.```mermaid sequenceDiagram autonumber Client->>API Gateway: POST /v1/orders API Gateway->>Kafka: Publish OrderCreated Event Kafka->>OrderWorker: Consume Event Moving Beyond Static AnnotationsFor APIs, we shifted the burden of maintenance entirely to self-documenting code. Rather than manually describing REST endpoints or gRPC contracts in a browser editor, we leveraged code-level annotations, such as OpenAPI and Swagger for REST services, or Protobuf definitions for gRPC. The beauty of this approach is that the API reference documentation generates itself during the build phase. When a developer adds or modifies an endpoint parameter in the codebase, the documentation updates automatically.Treating Docs Like Code in CI/CDTo guarantee quality, we began reviewing documentation in pull requests right alongside production code. We integrated lightweight documentation validation steps directly into our GitHub Actions pipeline. Automated linters immediately catch broken internal links, dead URLs, or bad formatting before code ever hits .Once a pull request merges, static site generators like MkDocs Material or Docusaurus automatically pull Markdown files across all our microservices and publish them to a single, beautifully organized, and searchable internal developer portal.Transitioning from a neglected wiki to a Code-First Docs model fundamentally reshaped our engineering culture.The most immediate win was in developer onboarding: new engineers went from struggling for two weeks with outdated setup steps to spinning up their local environments in under three days.Because documentation now lived right next to the code in pull requests, over 85% of architectural PRs began including matching file updates in the exact same commit.Perhaps best of all, we eliminated lost technical context. Every decision, rationale, and runbook update became fully searchable through and , giving engineers immediate insight into a system was built a certain way without needing to message a senior developer.Key Takeaways for Engineering TeamsIf you want to kill wiki rot in your organization, meet your developers where they already work. Forcing engineers to jump into an external browser portal guarantees documentation will eventually stall and decay.By pulling docs into the IDE, enforcing freshness through your CI/CD pipeline, and automating diagram generation directly from source code, you transform documentation from an annoying afterthought into a living asset that scales seamlessly with your codebase.

item.title: Reddit Is Getting a 'For You' Feed
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded: Reddit is overhauling its homepage with separate "For You" and "Following" feeds, with the former combining posts from subscribed communities and algorithmic recommendations based on users' interests and activity. The Verge reports: It's a big shift for the platform, but not an entirely surprising one, as Reddit hasn't been shy about wanting to switch up the homepage. Earlier this year, the company announced it would be deprecating r/all, which surfaced posts that were popular across the platform, as part of its "ongoing efforts to simplify Reddit and improve Home feed personalization." "This new feed experience is a first step in helping drive discovery that leads to something novel and relevant -- an idea, a connection, a unique perspective, or even a new interest," Reddit says. "A more human internet is not just something you sit back and watch, it is something you find value in and want to participate in."

item.title: 'Please Let the Internet Die'
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
Slashdot reader fjo3 shares an article from Wired: The internet must be put out of its misery. Any rational observer can admit that the current iteration of the web -- and the social fabric woven there -- is not what they signed up for. Symptoms of advanced cultural decay can no longer be ignored. This thing is eating itself. Giants including Meta and Google have been forced to settle massive consumer lawsuits brought over privacy violations and mental health harms allegedly caused by the addictive mechanisms of their platforms. Schools are banning smartphones as multiple countries institute social media restrictions for under-16s. Parents are in a panic about their kids aspiring to careers as social media celebrities, losing themselves in a vast ecosystem of online casinos, or joining extremist movements. Generative AI, briefly considered an amusing novelty, is now a turbocharged slop engine for the web, filling feeds and comment sections with useless, grotesque content. As humans scroll past headlines about AI taking their jobs, confusing fantasy for reality, and contributing to cognitive decline, any consumer appeal the technology might have is turning to anguish. The data centers that power it have become increasingly unpopular, and politically radioactive.
To be online, many now admit, is to be endlessly manipulated and exploited. In December, Oxford University Press declared rage bait to be the word of the year, noting that use of the term had tripled over the previous 12 months. The lexical spike represented a heightened awareness that monetized social accounts churn out bad-faith takes and extremist content, automating this abusive behavior with generative AI, simply to profit off hostile engagement. Billionaire oligarchs have opened the floodgates to such inauthentic activity, conspiracy-mongering, and hate speech by rolling back moderation. In short, when you hang around online in 2026, you see little worth saving. Perhaps a decade ago, you felt that the glimmers of community and joy, of artistic and intellectual exchange, were enough to balance out the toxic junk. No longer.

item.title: Hud Launches Agentic Rollouts to Move AI-Written Code From Pull Request to Production
item.author: Kevin John
item.content:encoded: has launched agentic rollouts, a new capability that helps coding agents move a code change from pull request to production while Hud validates each step against how that code actually behaves in live environments. The release targets what has become a major bottleneck in engineering: coding agents write a change in minutes, but that change can wait for days until there is enough confidence to ship it.With agentic rollouts, Hud analyzes every change before the merge, while the new version takes production traffic, and after the rollout. Safe pull requests can move forward at the pace agents produce them. When a change introduces a regression, Hud catches it, supports rollback or reversion, and hands the coding agent the context it needs to fix the issue and learn from it.According to Hud, the capability is now available to all its customers.Three Stages of ValidationAgentic rollouts are built on Hud's runtime code sensor, which teams add through a one-line SDK. The sensor automatically learns how backend code behaves in production at the function level, establishing a baseline that Hud then applies across the entire life of a change.Before the merge, Hud analyzes the pull request against a production impact map built from real parameters and code flows. It classifies the change by production risk level. When a change is flagged as risky, Hud supplies clear context so the review moves faster. A safe change can ship as fast as the agent wrote it.Once the new version begins taking traffic, Hud continuously compares its behavior to the established baseline. Regressions surface immediately. Because the analysis runs at the function level, Hud can identify both the root cause and the specific pull request responsible.If a regression occurs, Hud's context supports rolling back, reverting, and fixing the underlying issue. The coding agent receives deep context on what went wrong so it does not repeat the mistake.The result is that engineering teams can assess the production impact of changes before, during, and after they ship.Why the Launch Matters NowAI is increasingly part of engineers' daily workflows. shows that teams with high AI adoption merge 98% more pull requests, while pull request review time climbs 91%. In practical terms, engineers who lean heavily on AI produce roughly twice as many pull requests, and each one takes about twice as long to review.The delivery process has not kept up. According to, only 6% of organizations describe their continuous delivery as fully automated.That combination creates a bottleneck. Agents plan, write, and test code, then open a pull request within minutes. From there, the change waits for a person willing to merge it, because trusting an agent to ship without breaking production is difficult, and the agent has no visibility into how its code runs once deployed. Reviewers may approve pull requests they did not have time to read thoroughly, and someone has to monitor dashboards after each deploy. The more code agents write, the larger that backlog grows. Hud calls this gap the missing link in the AI software factory.Agentic rollouts are Hud's response to that gap. By validating every step against how the code actually runs in production, Hud aims to bring the speed of shipping closer to the speed of coding.Riverside Reverts Flawed Deploys in About Eight MinutesRiverside, the platform for recording and editing studio-quality audio and video, is among the companies running agentic rollouts. The company ships fast with AI, and much of its backend is real-time media code whose true behavior only appears under production load.Riverside sends every deploy through a canary, combined with Hud's agentic rollout and automatic rollback. According to, flawed deploys are detected quickly and reverted in about eight minutes on average, usually before a customer notices.Shilo Magen, VP of R&D at Riverside, said: "Our engineers use AI agents every day, and writing code is no longer the bottleneck. The real challenge is shipping that code to production with confidence.""For a real-time media platform like Riverside, even a small regression can have a major impact on the user experience. With Hud, we can automatically detect regressions and roll back problematic releases in minutes. Our engineers now spend less time worrying about deployments and more time building."Hud's CEO on Closing the GapRoee Adler, Co-Founder and CEO of Hud, framed the launch around the distance between writing code and shipping it."AI already changed how code gets written. The bigger problem now is getting that code into production safely, at the speed agents write it. Every engineering leader I talk to is trying to solve this problem. Coding and triage have agents, but the merge and rollout still run on people, because it's scary to give coding agents accountability over the stability and reliability of the production environment. That's the missing link in the AI software factory, and it's the problem we built Hud to solve. With agentic rollouts, agents and engineers work from the same runtime context, at the function level, so a change is merged to production based on evidence. When something does regress, it's immediately detected and fixed, but more importantly the agent that wrote it gets a feedback loop to learn and improve."That feedback loop reflects the direction Hud is building toward. Each rollout gives the coding agent information about how its changes behave in production, with the aim of reducing risk in subsequent changes.This article was published as a press release by the author under HackerNoon's program.

item.title: What Solana Staking Delegation Teaches Us About AI Agent Authority
item.author: Kenneth Onyebuchi
item.content:encoded: Solana gives you three ways to let someone else act on your funds, and each one grants a different power. A stake authority can point your stake at a validator but can never withdraw it. An SPL Token delegate can send your tokens to any address, up to a cap you set. A liquid staking pool takes your SOL into a program's custody and hands back a token. This piece compares what each model lets a delegate do, what the three have in common, and how the differences decide which one an AI agent that pays for its own compute should get.What Can a Stake Authority Do?Every Solana stake account has two authorities defined at creation: a stake authority and a withdraw authority. According to Solana's stake account documentation, the stake authority can delegate the account to a validator, deactivate it, split it, merge it, and assign a new stake authority. It cannot withdraw. The withdraw authority can withdraw undelegated SOL, assign a new withdraw authority, and reset the stake authority, which makes it the authority of last resort.A stolen stake authority key therefore lets an attacker deactivate your stake or move it between validators, which costs you rewards and time. The SOL stays in the account, and whoever holds the withdraw authority can replace the compromised stake authority.Marinade Native is a live example of this split. According to Marinade's native staking repository, the user keeps the withdraw authority while Marinade's program holds the stake authority. Marinade can direct the stake, and the owner can take the SOL back without Marinade's cooperation.What Can an SPL Token Delegate Do?A Solana token account can name one delegate and an allowance. Solana's spend permissions documentation describes the result: the delegate can transfer tokens out of the account up to the approved amount, and each transfer reduces the remaining allowance. The SPL Token program documentation adds that a delegate may transfer or burn up to the amount it was delegated, and it names that amount as the delegate's only limit, so the approval does not fix a destination. An account holds one active delegate at a time, and the owner's revoke instruction removes all of its permissions at once.This is a different power from a stake authority. A stake authority has no path to move funds to an address of its choosing, and an SPL delegate has exactly that, bounded by the cap. If a delegate key is stolen, the most an attacker can take is the remaining allowance. The cap is the whole safety mechanism, which makes its size the main design decision.Neither page describes an expiry. The documented ways an approval ends are revocation and the allowance reaching zero, so a time limit has to come from the owner revoking the approval or from a layer built on top of the token program.What Changes in a Liquid Staking Pool?Liquid staking moves custody. In Jito's design, depositors send SOL to a pool built on the SPL stake pool program, which holds the stake accounts and issues JitoSOL in return. Marinade Liquid runs on its own program rather than the SPL one and issues mSOL. In both pools the holder receives a claim token and no longer controls the authorities on any stake account.Exit works differently too. The owner of a stake account or a token allowance can cut off the delegate with one transaction. A pool holder leaves by redeeming or selling the token, which depends on the pool's liquidity and on the program continuing to behave as written. The trust sits in the code and in whoever can change it. Marinade's contract addresses page lists the Liquid program's upgrade authority as a 6-of-13 multisig.What Do the Three Models Share?Three properties hold across all of them:The owner's key stays the authority of last resort. The withdraw authority can reset the stake authority, a token owner can revoke or replace a delegate, and a pool holder keeps the right to redeem.The delegate's powers form a fixed list that the runtime or program enforces on every transaction.The damage from a compromised delegate is bounded by what it was granted.That third property is where the models diverge. A stake authority costs you rewards, an SPL delegate costs you the remaining allowance, and a pool's upgrade authority can reach every deposit in the pool.Delegate, deactivate, split, mergeTransfer or burn up to the allowanceHold stake accounts, issue a pool tokenCan it move funds to any address?Only as the program's code allowsWorst case if the key is stolenDepends on the program and its upgrade authorityReset the stake authority with the withdraw keyRedeem or sell the pool tokenDoes Delegating Stake Carry Risk?Delegating to a validator has not put principal at risk on Solana so far, because slashing is not live on the network. According to Everstake's overview, proposals to add it are still under discussion: SIMD-0204 would record evidence of slashable behavior and SIMD-0212 would set the penalties, which are not finalized. If slashing ships, a stake authority that picks a misbehaving validator could cost the owner part of the principal in addition to rewards, and the maximum loss for that model would no longer be rewards alone.Scale is easy to overstate, so here are the dated figures. DefiLlama lists Jito at about $1.108 billion in total value locked as of October 16, 2026, and Marinade at about $763 million as of October 17, 2026, roughly $1.87 billion combined. Marinade's figure combines its Native, Liquid, and Select products, and the Native portion stays in accounts whose withdraw authority belongs to users. Total value locked measures how much money relies on each design. It makes no statement about incident history, and I make no safety claim from it.Pick the narrowest primitive that matches the verb the agent needs: If the agent manages existing stake, such as choosing validators for a treasury, a stake authority gives it direction and no withdrawal power. If the agent pays invoices, such as a GPU marketplace bill, an SPL Token delegate with a cap sized to a billing period gives it spending power with a known maximum loss. If the agent needs a position that stays liquid, a pool token works, and the trust moves to the pool program and its upgrade authority.The spending case is the one most agent builders face first. Suppose an agent rents GPUs at $2 an hour and expects 40 hours of work a week. A weekly cap of $80 in a stablecoin means a leaked key costs at most $80 before the owner revokes it. A raw API key with no cap has no such number, which is the problem I described in an API key is not delegated authority. Because the base approval has no expiry, the owner also needs a routine that revokes or reduces the allowance at the end of each period.The stake authority is the best fit when an agent should never be able to move funds at all. A pool is the weakest fit for an agent that pays bills, because spending from a pool means redeeming first and the agent's risk then includes the pool's code.The useful question for an agent on Solana is which verb it needs, because each delegation model grants a different one. Size the grant to the loss you can absorb if the key leaks, and write that number down before you deploy. If you are building agent payments, start with an SPL Token delegate and a cap, then tell me in the comments what cap you would set for a week of GPU rental.
